In video processing tasks, identifying connections between nearby frames is crucial. Existing methods often employ sophisticated spatio-temporal convolutional networks but incur high computational costs and require a substantial amount of memory. This is because they usually treat neighboring frames as separate inputs and perform individual predictions, although they can leverage spatial correlations within video sequences. To address these issues, we propose PatchNet, a novel network design that efficiently combines nearby frames using short-range motion estimation through patch matching. This allows for shared-feature learning and reduced memory requirements. Furthermore, we introduce a PatchNet block, which can be used to develop video processing networks that are both computationally efficient and scalable. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, we tested PatchNet in a range of video prediction and analysis tasks and compared it against state-of-the-art video networks. The results show that PatchNet offers a significant reduction in computational requirements and memory needs without compromising its accuracy in handling video sequences. This makes it an ideal choice for video-centric AI applications, where handling short-range inter-frame connections is crucial. Instead, we delve into the detailed statistical properties of the system at specific non-equilibrium conditions. Our key discovery is the development of exact formulas for the system's multi-time distribution at various time increments. This achievement represents a significant advancement, as the associated mathematical evaluation yields explicit expressions for specific time periods, which, according to our analysis, exhibit distinct differences in behavior. Specifically, our results demonstrate that certain statistical properties exhibit complex and contrasting behaviors at certain time increments. In Fermi gases with a high number of components, characteristics that are typical of these systems in theoretical models often don't apply in real-life situations. Contrary to this trend, our research reveals that, in a specific type of Fermi gas, typical behavior is replaced by unusual properties. This type of Fermi gas is formed by combining large groups of fermions, and it exhibits pairing through a unique mathematical structure called SU(N) representations. Typically, in pairing systems, the excitation of a single mode per spin and momentum coordinate is possible; however, in the SU(N) Fermi gas, excitations are distributed across various modes, and this excitation type cannot be eliminated. As a result, unlike other pairing systems, the energy of the SU(N) Fermi gas pairing does not follow a simple mathematical structure. Through the use of a mathematical concept called degenerations, we show that, in the pairing system with the highest symmetry, a phase transition and a change in the pairing type are connected. This finding is unique because, in other systems, degenerations have only been used to understand properties of the system at zero temperature. Additionally, in another part of the research, we explore the effects of interactions that break symmetry on the pairing, and we show that, in the most symmetric system, a specific type of breaking does not affect the pairing type, and we describe how this system relates to a different physical system. Finally, in another part of the research, we establish relationships between different phases of another physical system, and we show how these relationships connect to another group of physical systems. This connection is particularly interesting because it shows how different physical systems that may seem very different are, in fact, connected. We establish a direct equivalence between the standard optomechanical cavity model and a modified electrical circuit model, based on the cavity-field formalism. The correspondence between these two formulations allows us, firstly, to demonstrate in an analytical manner that the usual optomechanical picture accurately replicates the behavior described by the complex electrical circuit model and, secondly, to explore the optical output field generated by the optomechanical cavity, taking into account both pure mechanical driving and hybrid electronic-mechanical driving. Additionally, we examine the influence of additional resistance in the electrical circuit, equivalent to internal photon and heater losses in the optomechanical cavity, on the antiphase modulation of the optical output field. Finally, we investigate how the amplitude of the induced current, associated with the mechanical driving frequency, is affected by the specific value of the mechanical resistance. Our analysis is ultimately performed for both the linear and nonlinear optomechanical cavity models, focusing on the hybrid driving case. The findings presented here enhance our understanding of the standard optomechanical picture and offer valuable insights into the optomechanical analysis, especially regarding the optomechanical tuning point, typically denoted as $\sim\beta_a$. The method used in this work can be applied to analyze optomechanical systems with other types of drives and should be useful in designing experiments to test the standard optomechanical picture, by replicating the electrical circuit model. Furthermore, we believe that the findings presented here could be translated into the domain of cold atoms, where the standard optomechanical picture is often applied, and, eventually, into the domain of condensed matter, where the standard optomechanical picture also holds great potential. In particular, we speculate that the induced current, associated with the mechanical driving frequency, could be probed using advanced techniques, such as high-resolution scanning tunneling spectroscopy. The ultimate goal is to induce current, associated with the mechanical driving frequency, on the single-photon level. The corresponding mechanical resistance value required to achieve this goal is estimated to be in the range of $\sim10^{10}$ Hz/s. The mechanical resistance value of $\sim10^{10}$ Hz/s is already reached with existing experimental setups, using techniques such as high-finesse micro-metals and/or topological insulators in an external magnetic field. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it is essential to accurately identify and track smoke presence. Although precision and reliability are critical considerations, current smoke detection methods lack them, solely providing prediction rates. In an attempt to overcome these shortcomings, we investigate the potential for pre-processing techniques to enhance laparoscopic video quality and improve smoke identification performance. Focusing on noise reduction, we evaluate the effectiveness of a data-driven approach, Middleton Filter, and a physics-based method, Lee Filter, and compare them to RGB and YUV color space conversions. Moreover, we introduce a novel, straightforward filter called Variance Filter, designed to capitalize on the distinct color patterns of smoke. By analyzing the results, we find that Variance Filter surpasses the performance of the other methods, and surprisingly, no image enhancement is required for smoke detection in laparoscopic surgery. This study's findings indicate that Variance Filter can serve as a reliable and efficient smoke detection method, and its success suggests that smoke patterns may be inherently interpretable. Furthermore, the variations in the color distributions of smoke and non-smoke images could be exploited to create effective filters. With the incorporation of a binary classifier, Variance Filter achieves precision, recall, and F1-score values of 0.940, 0.940, and 0.940, respectively. Additionally, we discover that combining the filters results in reduced computational complexity but minimal improved performance. Consequently, we propose Variance Filter as a streamlined and efficient smoke detection method, and suggest that image enhancement may not always be necessary for this task. This work has potential benefits for smoke removal techniques in surgical settings by providing an easily implementable and efficient method for smoke identification. In particular, Variance Filter could be adapted for real-time use on live surgical images to aid in smoke removal procedures. This could potentially improve visibility during laser ablation operations, enhancing the overall safety and effectiveness of the procedure. Leveraging deep learning models, we intend to explore the feasibility of applying Variance Filter as a pre-processing step, potentially utilizing transferred filters to enhance smoke detection. Compiling quantum circuits efficiently is crucial for achieving scalability in quantum computing. Currently available methods primarily focus on optimizing circuits with random gate sequences. However, emerging applications frequently produce circuits with recurring patterns, such as multiple repetitions of the same sequence. Existing methods are poorly suited to these types of circuits, resulting in elevated costs associated with compiling them. In this study, we present three deterministic techniques for abstracting and compiling circuits containing recurring patterns. We introduce a graph-based representation of recurring patterns, enabling the compilation of multiple sequence instances through a single process. We derive a method for generating low-depth circuit embeddings, where multiple instances of a pattern are concatenated. We also develop an algorithm combining low-depth circuit embeddings with transformation techniques to reduce circuit width, resulting in deeper circuits with reduced qubit counts. In terms of scalability, we apply an iterative process using a cover of minimal depth circuits to achieve low-depth compilations of circuits with recurring patterns. We evaluate our methods against state-of-the-art quantum circuit compilers, achieving better results in terms of compilation time and circuit depth, particularly for circuits with recurring patterns. We observe a compilation speed-up of one order of magnitude for patterns with two instances and increasing speed-up with the number of pattern instances for patterns with five and ten instances. Furthermore, we note a significant 10% average reduction in circuit depth for patterns with two instances and increasing depth reduction with the number of pattern instances. We believe these results will pave the way for efficient compilation of quantum algorithms with recurring patterns. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/qgreenecomp/repetitive-compilation. Recent breakthroughs in producing two-dimensional materials with an intrinsic dielectric layer have paved the way for achieving an excitonic insulator, a rare and complex quantum state that has not been observed in natural systems in over 80 years. A significant obstacle to realizing and studying this state is that it is typically located at extremely low temperatures and is prone to destruction by external vibrations. Our research utilizes a novel computational model to simulate the response of the excitonic system to the influence of phonons, and we find that the interaction with phonons results in the formation of tightly bound polaronic quasiparticles that retain the hallmark characteristics of the excitonic insulator even in the presence of significant vibration. Moreover, we determine that the energy spectrum of these polaronic quasiparticles exhibits a distinctive pattern of discrete energy levels that gradate into a band gap at low temperatures, and that the width of these energy levels is directly proportional to the strength of the phonon coupling. Our findings indicate that the spontaneous formation of polaronic quasiparticles could provide a viable mechanism for stabilizing the excitonic insulator and making it more amenable to experimental observation. Additionally, our research suggests that the ratio of the polaronic effective mass to the free electron mass can be accurately controlled and surpassed, a phenomenon unprecedented in modern two-dimensional materials. Our analysis also discloses that the mechanism driving the formation of polaronic quasiparticles is similar to that underlying ferromagnetism in spin-valve systems, and that the structural parameters of these systems can be tailored to produce a substantial enhancement of the exciton-phonon coupling strength, resulting in a significant decrease of the polaronic effective mass. Our research yields two novel guidelines for realizing an excitonic insulator in a double layer system via controlled parameter tuning: firstly, an increased value of the interlayer potential is required, and secondly, the valence and conduction bands of the system must cross over at an optimized point near the Fermi level. Our study offers a basis for a comprehensive understanding of the complex phenomenology of excitonic systems and provides a realistic framework for the development of novel quantum states. Additionally, our research paves the way for the utilization of polaron spectroscopy as an experimental tool to visualize the excitonic insulator and systematically investigate the parameters governing the exciton-phonon interaction in double layer systems. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that the implementation of polaron spectroscopy could facilitate the production of an excitonic insulator at temperatures significantly higher than those currently achievable

We establish a connection between orthomodular lattices and a specific type of topological space, specifically the 0-dimensional Hausdorff space. This relationship is based on a dual for orthomodular lattices, extending existing logical duals that preserve certain mathematical structures but not topological properties. Our method involves translating lattice operations into a combination of continuous functions, allowing us to construct a dual that preserves topological properties. This approach can be applied to other mathematical structures with logical implications, such as Heyting algebras. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the topological space obtained from this dual is unique and rich in structure, and that its continuous functions can be interpreted as orthomodular lattices. This is exemplified by an examination of the dual of the orthomodular lattice of subspaces of a finite-dimensional real vector space. This method can also be applied to other lattices with a logical interpretation. Specifically, we show that the dual of the lattice of compact open subspaces of a finite-dimensional real vector space topologically corresponds to the lattice of open subspaces, establishing a natural isomorphism between the dual of the orthomodular lattice and this latter lattice. This provides a topological reinterpretation of a previous logical analysis of orthomodular lattices. Our study also finds connections between geometric projections, which can be expressed as continuous functions, and set theoretic projections, which can be interpreted as topological mappings. Ultimately, we show that the dual of an orthomodular lattice is a 0-dimensional Hausdorff space, and that the continuous functions on this space can be interpreted as an orthomodular lattice. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Moreover, as the tool can generate visual representations, it is possible to employ PDF search functions to investigate the contents of proofs. Ultimately, this system's visual approach to proof scrutiny may offer insights into the reasoning processes underlying high-level mathematical objects. This research was influenced by our experiential insights into the benefits of visually presenting mathematical contents in the context of teaching and reviewing proofs. Consequently, we devised a proof visualization system that can translate $M$MetaCoq proof scripts into $\LaTeX$ or PDF files, thereby making it accessible to a broader audience. As this project's research outcome, we are sharing the companion website that includes documentation and the source code for this visualization system. It can be accessed at the specified URL. Furthermore, we have showcased the visual representations of eight notable proofs from the Coq Online Library, as well as forty intermediate level proofs from the Coq Cartography project. Nevertheless, a substantial portion of these proofs exhibit limited complexity in their structures; hence, there is a need for more diverse and complex evidence to validate the benefits of visualizing proofs. Moving forward, we propose the creation of a community-driven initiative, dubbed 'Visualising Coq Proofs', that invites contributors to participate by selecting and sharing the most compelling visual representations of proofs that can be accessed through a central repository. This project's success hinges on gathering a more diverse and extensive collection of proof visualizations, as well as fostering support among the Coq development team for incorporating the psv syntax as an official review tool. It is anticipated that the Visualising Coq Proofs initiative can serve as a flagship project, demonstrating the practical applications of interacting with the Coq proof tree in novel ways, as opposed to the existing hypertext-based review system. Moreover, this initiative could potentially leverage the resources and expertise of the wider mathematical community to create an invaluable collection of proof visualisations, thereby making it easier to learn, review and comprehend advanced mathematical concepts. This research outcome was presented at the Mathematical Structures for Secure Delegation workshop, as a oral presentation, as per the instructions

Furthermore, his conjecture holds true for forms associated with level one and also those that are square-free levels, except for the case of level two, which has been addressed by Hughes-Ramakrishnan in 2004. The key step in our proof involves establishing an asymptotic expression for the sum of the fourth powers of the eigenvalues of Hecke forms, which can be represented as level-dependent Fourier coefficients of specific cusp forms. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is used to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear system solver. However, the IPM's optimal convergence rate also depends on the linear equation solver's termination criterion. If the linear equation solver stops too late, it slows down the IPM, overriding the preconditioner's performance. We introduce a new termination criterion that dynamically adjusts the residual tolerance based on the Newton decomposition and optimal preconditioning. Combined with early termination and residual shifting, this "stop-when-inside-sufficiently-optimal" strategy enhances interior point methods by efficiently combining flexible preconditioning and optimal linear equation solving. We demonstrate numerical results confirming the performance boost compared to conventional methods. The code is available at https://github.com/marco-eis/StopInsideSOSO. The documentation can be found at marco-eis.github.io/StopInsideSOSO. The name "Stop Inside SOSO" (Stop Inside SubOptimal iterations for Optimal performances) reflects this inner loop dynamic. It is a play on words indicating a "good enough" inner loop solution is sufficient for an optimal overall behavior. The inner loop must not terminate too early because the outer loop needs some input, and it must not terminate too late because it means solving an inner loop again after each outer loop step, which results in worst case a quadratic number of inner loop steps. The name "SOSO" can also be interpreted as the inner loop's (lack of) quality. The goal is to reach a SOSO state as soon as possible which means a state where the inner loop's quality is minimal. The name "Stop Inside SOSO" captures the essential insight that an optimal termination criterion in interior point methods relies on reaching a state where the inner loop's performance degradation stops (insides SOSO). A recent breakthrough in RENOGFIL combines the principles of renormalization and gradient flows to create a flow that reaches its fixed point at a ultra-violet (UV) stable point, either a genuine fixed point or a limit cycle, within a finite number of steps. We develop various applications of this technique in both perturbative and solvable models, such as quantum electrodynamics in 2D and the 3D Ising model's low-temperature expansion. Additionally, we investigate how the UV stable point is reached synthetically via an artificial neural network trained with random data. Furthermore, we discover that the renormalization group flow can be captured through a series of small perturbations in the neighborhood of the UV stable point, leading to a deep understanding of the critical surface. Lastly, we explore the mapping between the renormalization group flow and the dynamics of a classical lattice gas, revealing a potentially link between quantum field theories and classical statistical models. Our work introduces and demonstrates a novel method for tackling renormalization group problems, showcasing its versatility in a range of scenarios. It also raises intriguing questions about potential connections between gradient flow and renormalization, as well as the statistical mechanics of driven systems. Crucially, the UV stable point is reached naturally, either through an infinite number of steps or through training of an artificial neural network, rendering the technique intrinsically UV complete. We push the technique to read off critical exponents, Wess-Zumino terms, and low-energy effective actions, offering fresh insights into their behavior. In particular, we derive the low-energy effective action to high order for the 3D Ising model's low-temperature expansion, yielding a surprise discovery about the low-energy expansion's behavior. Our technique's UV completeness is crucial in understanding this result. Furthermore, we investigate the low-temperature expansion of the quantum field theory describing an impurity in the Kondo problem, revealing a novel discrepancy with existing results. Our technique introduces a novel method to tackle such quantum field theories, offering fresh insights into their behavior. We explore the possibility of training artificial neural networks not just with random data but with samples drawn from the distribution of flatus, exhaled by humans while watching renormalization group flows. We discover that this leads to a significant acceleration in reaching the UV stable point, rendering such models intrinsically UV complete. Our work offers fresh perspectives on fundamental questions in physics, such as the nature of quantum field theories at low temperatures and the origin of entanglement in the ground state

Current business process monitoring methods primarily focus on model-based approaches, which have limitations when processes deviate from their predefined models, as they typically only capture a specific process definition. To address this issue, this work introduces a method for monitoring process executions aligned with predefined models, using both data and control flow rules. This involves defining a process model as a combination of correct and incorrect execution paths, some of which may not be representable through a traditional process model. We propose an automata-theoretic model, enabling the identification of all possible process executions, regardless of their validity. To address model inconsistencies, this method incorporates a conflict management mechanism, allowing for the resolution of incompatibilities between allowed transition paths. The efficacy of this monitoring method is demonstrated through an example scenario in the healthcare industry. Furthermore, this method's feasibility is validated through an experimental evaluation of its performance using real-world process models. Results indicate that the proposed monitoring method performs adequately, given the model's size. Details regarding the implementation and experimental setup can be found in an accompanying document. Additionally, a monitoring tool based on this method is available for public access, along with an example process model illustrating its capabilities. This process model showcases a healthcare procedure with predefined and incorrect execution paths, as well as invalid transition patterns that require conflict resolution. We exemplify conflict resolution for specific process execution IDs. Moreover, this work presents an expanded version of the model, incorporating 12 transition types, as well as an automaton-based model, enabling the identification of all possible process executions. These executions are categorized into valid and invalid types. The proposed monitoring method enables the identification of all incorrect process executions at a specific execution stage, utilizing their corresponding execution IDs and transition types. We demonstrate this method's efficiency through a comparative analysis with other monitoring methods, highlighting its distinct capabilities. Finally, this work addresses practical concerns regarding model inconsistencies, conflicts, and invalid process executions, ultimately leading to the development of the proposed monitoring method. A possible conflict resolution strategy is also presented, along with a more detailed explanation of this approach's capabilities. In summary, this work presents a novel process monitoring method, addressing model inconsistencies, conflicts, and invalid process executions. The efficacy and feasibility of this method are validated through empirical evaluations, utilizing real-world process models and empirical data to compare its performance with other existing monitoring methods. The proposed monitoring method, along with accompanying process models and execution data, are available for public access. Quipper, a domain-specific language, enables the description of quantum circuits through embedded languages integrated into functional languages like Haskell. These embedded languages, known as DSLs, facilitate the compilation of quantum circuits into efficient, targeted low-level codes. The evolving nature of quantum computing hardware, however, necessitates a more agile description system capable of adapting easily to changing target hardware. The Embedded Quantum Hardware Description Language, eQHDL, addresses this need by allowing the description of quantum hardware through first-order functional languages. Despite its benefits, describing the full details of quantum hardware within a single description becomes cumbersome and computationally expensive. To resolve this limitation, we introduce proto-Quipper-M, an extension of Quipper that incorporates the eQHDL and employs abstract state machines to represent complex quantum hardware systems. The abstract state machine provides a modular framework that enables the description of different hardware components without compromising computational efficiency. Furthermore, we outline a sound proof for the semantic definition of proto-Quipper-M based on a standard framework for functional programming languages. This new direction in Quipper research enables the description of quantum hardware systems at a higher level of abstraction, promoting greater agility in adapting to advancing quantum computing hardware. The resulting descriptions, encompassing both quantum circuits and complex hardware systems, become more accessible and easier to understand due to the introduction of abstract state machines. Consequently, this facilitates easier reasoning about the overall behavior of quantum algorithms. We showcase the efficacy of proto-Quipper-M by applying it to two specific use cases, the solvation model and the surface code, which highlight its capabilities and potential applications. Ultimately, this research brings Quipper and its extensions one step closer to the broader quantum algorithm paradigm known as quantum software engineering. The approach could lead to the automatic generation of quantum software based on the detailed description of quantum hardware. The proto-Quipper-M extension is available through the Quipper GitHub repository. Additionally, we provide a separate interface for the abstract state machine, as well as the eqhdls used in this research. You can access the GitHub repository at: https://github.com/quiphera/quiphera-pqm and view the repository for the abstract state machine and eqhdls at: https://github.com/quiphera/asm-quipper-pqm and https://github.com/quiphera/pq-m-eqhdls. respectively. This scaling impact a broad range of statistical properties, influencing the distribution of secondary extremes and their associated number, a count that's currently inaccessible through existing theoretical analysis. This work employs a novel approach, involving a randomly truncated parabola, to derive a precise formula for the distribution of secondary extremes in the scaling regime. This distribution is found to transition from a Gaussian form in smaller sizes to a Cauchy form in larger sizes. Furthermore, the study reveals that secondary extremes follow a volume law, meaning their number grows proportionally to the size of the matrices, and identifies various scaling regimes for the distribution of secondary extremes, characterized by distinct power-law behaviors. In contrast to random matrix theory, an analogous approach and results are obtained for the eigenvalues of a specific type of Wigner matrix, a matrix based on the parabolic hypothesis, and the findings indicate a profound connection between the two systems. This connection enables the derivation of a precise formula for the distribution of secondary extremes in the scaling regime in a related type of Wigner matrix, a result previously unknown in the field. We suggest creating entangled bosonic systems within optical lattices formed by ensembles of rare-earth ions in optical microcells. The work begins with a review of previous research demonstrating the optical manipulation of a single pair of praseodymium ions in a cavity for the purpose of measuring phase. We expand on this research by outlining a feasible approach to generate entangled pairs on a larger scale, suitable for applications in quantum information technology. The scale-up involves introducing a method to produce numerous pairs within an ensemble of Ho+ ions, with the goal of utilizing their two-body interactions to form correlated states. However, this approach proves to be impractical due to an increased risk of decoherence. As an alternative, we present a scheme for the production of entangled bosonic systems using the cavity-microsphere configuration and utilizing the differential cavity coupling of rare-earth ions, with a specific focus on erbium ions. The proposal incorporates a combination of optical manipulation, two-photon transitions, and Rayleigh scattering to generate a pair of entangled photons and places the system within an optical cavity to enhance photon interaction. The entangled pair can be generated through the application of a single optical pulse, resulting in the creation of a squeezed state, with a subsequent cooling process using a second tone pipe to produce a truly twofold degenerate state suitable for phase measurement. The proposed plan is feasible for practical implementation and could serve as a key component in future quantum information technology and quantum metrology applications. The potential for observing entangled correlations is discussed, with predictions outlined for future experimental observation. The entanglement and squeezing in this system far surpass the limitations imposed by cavity bandwidth, with potential applications in optical metrology that extend beyond current scale limitations. The proposal includes a method for determining the entanglement parameters $\chi$ and $\zeta$, with a particular consideration given to the effects of spontaneous photon emission and Rayleigh scattering. The overall approach is versatile, with the possibility of adapting it to other collections of ions, such as thulium, with slightly modified optical manipulation techniques. The proposal potentially enables the development of the most highly squeezed states available for measurement, with a great deal of flexibility in choosing the ensemble for the application. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and edge-adjacency lists, to create contiguous, overlapping DNA sequences within a distributed-memory environment. By applying graph partitioning and sequence alignment, sequential and sequential-offloading strategies are implemented to contribute to the assembly's progress. Furthermore, through comprehensive experiments including real-world genomes, the proposed approach's efficiency and effectiveness are evaluated and optimized. It achieves speeds of up to 396 MB/s on the IBM Lenovi cluster, outperforming existing serial methods by 12 to 20 times. Additionally, the results show that the assembly quality remains comparable to that of conventional, serial approaches with the help of internal overlap verification. Therefore, the proposed approach offers a substantial performance boost with minimal impact on assembly accuracy. It has the potential to significantly contribute to genome assembly projects by accelerating contig creation. These assemblies can then be used to inform various applications in genomics, such as identifying disease-causing mutations, studying genome evolution, and confirming therapeutic targets. Recently, a method was proposed to extend the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation to point processes, but it didn't take into consideration the fact that the ILR transformation depends on the composition of the measure's atoms. Therefore, defining a suitable measure that captures the hierarchical structure and allowing the ILR transformation to be dependent on this structure is essential. Our study introduces a new approach to deep point processes that uses a distance metric based on the ILR transformation, thereby enabling the description of a measure's hierarchical structure. We utilize this idea to develop a point process depth that is based on the notion of semi-variance, ultimately allowing us to identify the most important components and the temporal patterns within them. We test our new method in various simulation studies and real-world data analysis scenarios to validate its effectiveness. The proposed approach is also available under an open-source license. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/krishnanarayanan-krishnan/ILRDepth. A detailed explanation of the method and its accompanying data files are also available at https://krishnanarayanan-krishnan.github.io/ILRDepth/. The website includes a set of guided instructions and additional details on how to apply the method to spatial point processes data. Our initial findings of 66Ge's gamma-ray decay mode from 66Ga's beta-plus capture process have prompted us to investigate nuclear properties at the $N$ = 40 island of inversion. Structural analyses across the island, encompassing 46Ga, 50Zr, 52Kr, 54Se, 54Ge, 56As, and 56Se, demonstrate that an significant energy gain occurs at the $N$ = 40 shell threshold, resulting in shortened deformation lengths and increased deformation magnitudes for 54Ge and 56As, whereas 46Ga exhibits spherical character. Despite sitting near the dripline, 54Ge's 2+ state exhibits essentially the same energy as 52Kr's, suggesting that unpaired protons and neutrons' rotational coupling causes this state to be broadly based. New (20 GHz) atomic beam hyperfine microwave spectroscopy has been carried out on 54Ge, yielding newly determined nuclear properties, including magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments. Relating ground-state properties to isotones reveals an M1 transition pattern featuring increasing strength for 54Ge and decreasing strength for 56As, prompting discussion of the phenomenon's cause. Additionally, 54Ge's half-life has been estimated (4.6 millisecond) by analyzing 54Ge's beta-plus decay to 54Se in conjunction with 54Ga's beta-plus capture process. Experimental data are compared with the results of large-scale shell model calculations which accurately predict ground-state properties, including deformation and spin-isospin properties. However, shell model calculations that account for stripped surface factors and structured correlations yield superior agreement with observed transition patterns. Moreover, shell model calculations facilitate a deeper understanding of the island of inversion, including the nature of low-lying collectives and coupled rotors across the island, as well as novel phenomena like rotational coupling between unpaired protons and neutrons in 54Ge. Finally, applied nuclear moments derived from 54Ge's spectroscopy are presented, including an estimated magnetic dipole moment for the 56As ground state. The study provides a comprehensive nuclear portrait for 54Ge, serving as a reference point for nuclear structure and potentially informing astrophysical reactions. Moreover, 54Ge's properties are anticipated to enhance our understanding of similar Se isotopes and the island of inversion in general, as well as the Se hypermultiplet, which is a subject of ongoing nuclear research. Finally, nuclear moment applications, including atomic beam hyperfine microwave spectroscopy, are discussed

Our novel approach, called "Regular Expression Biasing," renders models more biased towards predicted results within specified patterns, essentially making them more confident in expected outcomes. This paper showcases the effectiveness of REB on the task of structured text recognition, demonstrating its capability to boost accuracy on datasets with diverse formats and simplicity levels. Furthermore, we introduce a novel dataset featuring a wide array of structured text formats, referred to as the "Structured Text Recognition Dataset (STRD)." The difficulty arises from the diverse range of expressions used to convey similar meanings in different domains. Currently, approaches relying solely on sequential data are ineffective due to their inability to capture syntactic variations, while models incorporating visual knowledge have shown improved performance but often require time-consuming and labor-intensive annotations. We propose an innovative method that leverages cross-domain translation to enhance sentence-level translation within a specific domain by utilizing unlabelled data from other domains through an auxiliary task. This auxiliary task employs pre-trained models to generate fake SQL data, which serves as a pseudo-label to update the main model's parameters. As a result, the end-to-end system achieves better performance on SP-SST2, a dataset consisting of SQL queries within the SQL database domain. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset, MD-SST2, comprising three domains (menu description, product description, and recipe), and evaluate our proposed method alongside eight baseline models on four diverse domains, demonstrating superior performance across all domains. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been successful in feature selection and model estimation. However, its original standard interior-point method experienced a significant increase in computational time with the growth of problem size. In response to this limitation, an inner-point adaptive-sieving algorithm is presented, based on a novel reformulation of the HDR Lasso problem. This new approach integrates a tailored adaptive-sieving algorithm to solve a continuous sub-problem, providing substantial speed improvements while maintaining equivalent solution quality to the inner-point method. Furthermore, extensive numerical studies demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness across a range of experimental settings. Additionally, our open-source R software is meticulously developed for user convenience. This package complements our recent research on sLasso and eLasso problems, ComPCo, allowing users to access a collection of useful tools and functionality. This includes support for both continuous and discrete sub-problems, along with the capability to specify custom data matrices. This R software not only replicates but also enhances the performance of the presented algorithm. As such, the provided solution algorithm can serve as a reliable resource for data analysts and researchers tackling HDR Lasso-related problems arising from high-dimensional regression and their associated computational challenges. Details regarding our software package can be found at: https://github.com/tieunguo/ComPCo/tree/main/ComPCo_R. The fluctuation theorem's extended version predicts a relation between entropy production and asymmetry in probability distributions for systems driven far from equilibrium. This relation holds universally, regardless of any specific details of the driving protocol. We examine whether this truth extends to individual driving sequences or if it's specific to continuously changing drivings. For a simple model, we investigate the difference between these two scenarios. The results show that some aspects of the fluctuation theorem apply broadly, while others depend on the driving protocol's details. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings on the convexity of the entropy production function and show that certain assumptions about its curvature are too broad. The analysis reveals that the fluctuation theorem's structure is reflected in the functional form of the entropy production function, demonstrating the complexity of thermodynamics that arises from probabilistic considerations. Additionally, we identify a crucial condition for the applicability of the fluctuation theorem, which must be met for the entropy production to be accurately measured. This condition involves the slow correlation of system and thermal motion, governed by the system's relaxation time and its mean free path. Based on these findings, we distinguish between thermodynamic force and the fluctuating force, which are unable to be distinguished experimentally. The study's conclusions are relevant to a wide range of driven systems, including biological membranes, electrical circuits, and radioactive decays, and suggest a general approach to verifying the fluctuation theorem in various experiments. The analysis also raises fundamental questions about the thermodynamic description of individual driving sequences and the underlying microscopic mechanisms that give rise to the observed probabilistic correlations. Furthermore, it highlights the distinction between thermodynamic description and the fluctuation theorem, which are not interchangeable. This observation suggests that some aspects of modern thermodynamics may require revision in light of the emerging understanding of entropy production and the fluctuation theorem. This paper introduces a new model that explores how individuals form and express opinions within a complex network of interconnected relationships. We have developed a theoretical framework, referred to as the Limited Confidence Model (LCM), based on structural balance theory. We have demonstrated that LCM captures key aspects of real-world opinion dynamics, including the emergence of polarized groups and the decline of moderate viewpoints. Additionally, we have shown that the dynamic interplay between opinion and social relationships results in the fragmentation of smaller groups within a large network. We employ both numerical simulations and empirical analysis to validate the effectiveness of LCM. We have conducted an experiment testing the model's relevance in an online setting, where participants engaged with a group discussion moderated by a complex network and guided by LCM rules. The resulting data from this study align closely with the model's predicted outcomes, underscoring the relevance of LCM in understanding human interaction dynamics. By modeling opinion dynamics through the interplay between confidence and structural balance, LCM provides a comprehensive approach to studying the interconnected development of group attitudes and social relationships. LCM offers a potential framework for designing interventions that could promote diverse perspectives, reduce extreme views, and foster a more cohesive social environment. LCM also presents an opportunity to explore its applications in fields such as social media moderation, group therapy, and conflict resolution. Different genes exhibit varying speeds of transcription, with some producing the same amount of mRNA in a shorter time frame as others that take a longer time. To understand the mechanisms behind these varying speeds, researchers created a model that predicts the timing of mRNA production based on genetic information and compared it to real-time data on mRNA levels in cells. This model allowed them to identify patterns of repeated sequences within genes, slow production of mRNA, and to make predictions about the effects of changes in the sequence on transcription speed. This predicted model accurately accounted for most of the changes in mRNA levels, revealing a complex interplay between sequence and the timing of mRNA production. Furthermore, by focusing on genes encoding proteins involved in DNA repair, researchers discovered that increasing the speed of transcription by removing pauses can boost the repair efficiency by as much as five times. This study demonstrates a method to systematically analyze the mechanics of transcription and reveals the significance of pauses in gene expression in the performance of cellular functions. Ultimately, this research enables the optimization of gene expression to enhance cellular processes. Automatically creating code based on visual information has been a major challenge in the field of program generation. A new approach is being taken by researchers to develop algorithms that can translate flow charts directly into executable programs. Previous attempts to address this task have been hindered by the reliance on predetermined program templates and limited model complexity. In an effort to overcome these obstacles, a new model called GRCNN is being presented - a graph recognition convolutional neural network designed to generate programs from flow charts without any pre-defined templates. By leveraging a vast dataset of hand-annotated flow charts and corresponding programs, GRCNN is being trained to recognize and generate programs from unfamiliar diagrams. Furthermore, novel experiments demonstrate the ability of GRCNN to produce accurate and functional programs on its own, achieving unprecedented levels of performance compared to previous approaches. In particular, generated programs on a benchmark dataset demonstrate a 94.5% accuracy in executing successfully, marking a substantial improvement over existing solutions. A comprehensive evaluation of GRCNN also highlights its superiority over alternative approaches in multiple evaluations. By pushing the boundaries of what is possible in program generation, this work opens the door for future research to build on its achievements and achieve more sophisticated outcomes. The study of the gastrointestinal tract is crucial for understanding digestive functions and pathologies, yet its investigation poses significant technical challenges due to its complex anatomy and the various diseases that affect it. Advances in image processing and analysis via computational methods have made significant contributions in this field, enabling researchers to tackle more complex problems. Segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract from imaging data is a vital component of computational gastroenterology, allowing for the identification and tracking of anatomical structures and alterations caused by disease or treatment. While manual segmentation using expert input can be efficient for smaller datasets, it becomes impractical for larger image collections. In response, researchers have developed and evaluated various semantic segmentation algorithms for gastrointestinal imaging applications. This study compares multiple state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for automatic gastrointestinal region segmentation using publicly accessible imaging datasets. Despite achieving promising results, several challenges persist, such as dealing with diverse acquisition devices, clinical pathways, and the variability of lesions and internal organs. To overcome these obstacles, the research community needs to collaborate and develop more robust, flexible, and adaptable methods that can incorporate context from different clinical settings. Future developments could incorporate task-specific constraints, incorporating experts' knowledge and semi- and unsupervised learning techniques to expand the usability of segmentation models across various institutions and applications. Lastly, integrating these segmentation models into clinical practice requires further context, such as lesion classification, growth tracking, and treatment assessment, to name a few examples. This study serves as a starting point for investigating automatic gastrointestinal region segmentation through the collaborative effort of the computer vision and biomedical imaging research community. Leveraging computational methods to study the gastrointestinal system holds great potential for advancing individualized medicine, boosting medical research, and making medical training more effective. Compositional data are mathematical expressions that represent the combination of components within an object or system, with each component being a percentage or fraction of the whole. They are commonly described by multivariate data sets where observations are linear combinations of positive coefficients that sum to a constant value. These data sets are frequently encountered in various disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the life sciences. The unique characteristics of compositional data necessitate specialized analytical methods. This article discusses how linear algebra can inform our understanding and analysis of compositional data. We then explore how visualization techniques can further detail the information contained within these data and highlight the challenges associated with interpreting results. Ultimately, we emphasize the importance of communicating findings effectively to the broader scientific community. To showcase our approaches, we utilize the CoxBio library, which incorporates the CoxPalm library, to analyze artificial compositional data resulting from the mixing of artificial components. The search for planets with sub-Saturn masses within specific metallicity ranges is ongoing in several exoplanet surveys, as current findings are inconsistent across different projects. We have analyzed a sample of 254 planets from radial velocity measurements, focusing on those with masses between 10 M_E and 100 M_E, and metallicities between 0.1 M_E/sol to 5 M_E/sol. In contrast to previous studies, our analysis found no evidence that planet formation is impeded or slowed down for masses between 10 M_J and 100 M_J, across all metallicity levels. According to our statistical analysis, the completion of the radial velocity follow-up program for the HARPS sample planets should likely rule out the concept of a 'planet desert' or significant slowdown in planet formation recovery for masses between 10 M_J and 100 M_J, across a wide range of metallicity levels. However, the study is unable to rule out the idea of a 'planet desert' or significant slowdown in planet formation recovery for masses between 0.3 M_Saturn and 1 M_Saturn, across a narrow range of super-Saturn mass threshold. Future studies utilizing data from other radial velocity samples are required to further validate these conclusions and investigate the phenomenon of a 'planet desert' or significant slowdown in planet formation recovery around super-Saturn mass threshold. We have also identified key statistical biases that affect planet detection and completion of follow-up for the HARPS sample, which are likely to be present in other radial velocity samples as well. These biases are related to the relationship between planet mass and its orbital period, as well as the metallicity of the host star. Consequently, the detection and completion of follow-up for the HARPS sample showed a notable preference for more massive giant planets with longer orbital periods and those orbiting more metal-rich stars. We have also analyzed the underlying distribution of planet mass and period biases and found that the radial velocity sample follows a common pattern, characterized by a steep increase in planet mass with its orbital period. Notably, the radial velocity sample demonstrates distinct behavior in different periods, as planets with shorter orbital periods are more abundant at lower masses, while those with longer orbital periods are more abundant at higher masses. Intelligent systems that interact with unpredictable environments require adaptable attention mechanisms to collect relevant information from their surroundings. Unfortunately, existing attention methods are often undermined by external interference. To tackle this challenge, we have developed a novel, robust attention control system that can filter out unnecessary information and prioritize relevant data collection. This goal is achieved by optimizing a mutually informative connection between the attention module and the data source, specifically the agent's memory. As a result, the attention module is trained to effectively extract meaningful information from the data source while remaining immune to external interference. To accomplish this, we designed a specific mutual information estimation technique that simplifies the process of optimizing mutual information. Our proposed method was successfully tested in a challenging scenario where an intelligent system navigates a dynamic environment and collects relevant information. Notably, the attention mechanism was able to effectively isolate the relevant information from the data source, even in the presence of external interference. This is evident in our experimental results, which demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method when compared to alternative techniques. Ultimately, the attention mechanism was able to collect more informative data and achieve better outcome rewards. A video showcasing the method in action can be found on our website. This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image intensity inversion. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, direction, normal, and intensity variation trend) generates features that are robust to spatial inversions and intensity reversals. These enhanced feature properties contribute to the development of a symmetric image registration framework, incorporating SIFT-like geometric features and utilizing the National Library of Medicine's ANTS software. This registration framework is evaluated on specific tasks, including registering neuroimaging data and synthesizing head CT scans from MRI scans, both of which are insensitive to image inversion and 3D transformations, demonstrating higher robustness and accuracy in challenging conditions. Global pooling techniques, such as average pooling and global average pooling in CNNs, are often considered to be simplistic and lacking in representational power. In contrast, we show that these layers are complex and demanding to approximate. By framing global pooling in terms of optimal transport theory, we find that averaging operators are among the most efficient means of achieving a low-cost, unitary transformation of input images. Due to their efficiency, these layers are resistant to approximation by more complex architectures, such as CNNs with multiple nonlinear layers. Our findings are corroborated by a range of challenging tasks and diverse datasets, where we find that CNNs with global pooling consistently outperform more complex architectures. Ultimately, our work highlights the importance of seeking interpretations and theoretical justifications for the designs of neural networks. The code to reproduce our results can be accessed at https://github.com/keunlee/Global-Pooling-through-Optimal-Transport. Jelassi et al. introduced the concept of optimal transport (OT) as a tool for understanding image transformations. OT can describe a wide range of transformations, including nonlinear ones, and OT-based models achieve exceptional performance on 1D classification tasks. However, OT-based models are often computationally expensive and difficult to differentiate. In response to these challenges, researchers have proposed various approximations to OT. Our study begins by examining global pooling (GP) through the lens of OT, and we find that GP approximately achieves a low-cost, unitary transformation of input images. We find that GPs are highly efficient and resistant to approximation by more complex architectures. Our analysis is corroborated by a range of experiments, in which we find that CNNs with GP consistently outperform more complex architectures. We investigate the relationship between OT-based models and GP, and we find that OT-based models can be approximated by CNNs with GP. Our results are corroborated by a range of experiments, in which we find that CNNs with GP consistently outperform OT-based models on tasks involving multiple inputs and diverse datasets. Ultimately, we highlight the importance of seeking interpretations and theoretical justifications for the designs of neural networks. The code to reproduce our results can be accessed at https://github.com/keunlee/Global-Pooling-through-Optimal-Transport. One simple yet effective layer in CNNs is global pooling (GP), and we examine the conceptual underpinnings of GP by framing it within the context of optimal transport. We find that OT-based models, including GP, can achieve exceptional performance on 1D classification tasks

The study of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is rich in diversity, encompassing a broad spectrum from high-energy extragalactic light sources to massive black holes residing at the centers of galaxies. By examining the characteristics of AGNs based on their spectral properties and the properties of their host galaxies, researchers can gain insight into their underlying mechanisms and historical galaxy-evolution processes. Prior studies focusing on galaxy properties used somewhat outdated classification methods for AGNs, defined solely by their hard and soft X-ray ratios, which failed to consider many significant aspects. Conversely, studies focusing on hard X-rays alone were unable to explore the diverse nature of AGNs. To address these limitations, a comprehensive study classified AGNs using hard X-ray emission lines and investigated their relationships with host-galaxy properties. Notably, the research found that the hard X-ray emission patterns of radio-loud AGNs differed significantly from those of radio-quiet AGNs, while also uncovering distinct patterns in their host-galaxy properties. Furthermore, the investigation revealed that the sample of radio-loud AGNs displayed greater variability in their hard X-ray emission and harder continuum spectra compared to radio-quiet AGNs. Additionally, the study found that the black-hole masses of radio-loud AGNs were much higher, by a factor of 10, than those of radio-quiet AGNs, which is consistent with their greater galaxy luminosities and larger sizes. Most radio-loud AGNs were found to exist in an advanced stage, with their galaxies characterized by large sizes, high star-forming rates, and prominent dust content. Conversely, the sample of narrow-line radio-quiet AGNs displayed smaller host galaxies marked by low star-forming rates and reduced dust content. Notably, the study also differed from previous findings by failing to uncover notable differences in the bulge-to-disk ratios of broad-line AGNs, while also not observing previously reported relationships between black-hole mass and hard X-ray emission or soft X-ray excess. These results were likely the result of using broadband X-ray data, as employing both broadband and high-resolution spectrometers are essential for uncovering the complex physical processes within the AGN itself and its host galaxy. The study is a significant step towards elucidating the underlying coevolutionary processes between AGNs and their host galaxies by enabling researchers to examine the diverse nature of various AGN types using galaxy properties. The rise of AI-powered voice assistants and smart speakers has created new opportunities for developing systems that can automatically create audio or spoken content from written text. Currently, there is a disconnect between the various techniques used for different components of speech synthesis. Our work addresses this gap by proposing TCube, a unified neural framework that streamlines spoken content generation. TCube features a dual-stream architecture, processing input in two ways: (1) a semantic stream analyzing the content's meaning and (2) a prosodic stream generating the soundtrack. Our system uses two separate neural networks to produce audio, one focused on melody and rhythm and the other on spectral features. Our results show that TCube's audio samples are indistinguishable from professionally recorded ones, earning high marks from human listeners for their authenticity and pleasure value. Our method even surpasses established speech synthesis systems while using fewer resources, thereby paving the way for new spoken content generation methods. Our speech synthesis dataset, "Content-Based Speech Synthesis," can be found at this link: https://tinyurl.com/CBSS2022. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved significant insights into the properties of beauty mesons, including their rare and unusual decays. This paper provides an overview of recent findings on decays involving the violation of CP symmetry (left-right asymmetry) and infrequent transformations in beauty mesons. Data analyzed from 7 and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions, totalling 4.6 inverse femtobarns of branching data, have been used to extract experimental values of branching ratios, asymmetries, and other key observables. These measurements have subsequently been compared with theoretical predictions based on the standard model of particle physics. Additionally, the paper discusses how these measurements contribute to our understanding of the standard model and sets limits on the existence of beyond-standard-model interactions. Finally, the paper outlines future plans for analyzing data collected during the LHC's Run 2. The combined collection of 26 inverse femtobarns of branching data will significantly enhance precision, enabling the measurement of many beauty meson decays for the first time and allowing the standard model to be tested at an even more rigorous level. The paper also presents new findings on the decay of the charm particle system $B^0_s$ to a kaon and a muon, along with an exploration of its directional separation. The analysis of this process, governed by the CKM factor $B(L)_s$, has led to the measurement of its absolute value, $|B(L)_s|$, and an extraction of the angle $\beta_s$, a key component in the charmed quark system. The paper also reports on studies of uncommon beauty meson decays, such as the decay of the meson system $B^0_d$ to a kaon and an electron, along with analyses involving particle tagging to determine the nature of its counterpart decay. The measurement of this rare transformation, involving the weak force, has led to the setting of limits on its occurrence and the confirmation of its non-existence to a particular kaon and electron pair. The paper also discusses future plans for enhancing these limits, utilizing data collected during the LHC's Run 2. The analysis has also been explored for measuring entangled states in unconnected beauty meson pairs and the interference between the decay of the meson system $B^0_d$ to a kaon and a muon, along with its counterpart decay via the weak force. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and examine its potential Gibbs states. These states can be categorized into two types: strongly periodic states, and weakly periodic states. The study focuses on evaluating the thermodynamic properties of the latter. We have successfully designed two periodic extensions of the Ising model's Hamiltonian, and computed their corresponding free energies, thus ensuring the existence of these weakly periodic Gibbs states. This achievement is unprecedented, as previously, experts were only able to demonstrate the existence of periodic Gibbs states on trees that were strongly periodic. We have also investigated the phase transitions associated with these new Gibbs states. One of the periodic extensions exhibits a second-order phase transition, marked by a continuous temperature variation in its magnetization. This transition occurs at a specific temperature that diminishes as the tree's size increases. Conversely, the other extension exhibits a first-order phase transition, characterized by the appearance of multiple magnetization levels with varying spin orientations. This transition is also accompanied by the formation of a spin flip barrier, evaluated as a difference in magnetization energy between adjacent states. This study enhances our understanding of Gibbs states and their thermodynamic applications, using a tree structure as a testing ground. One potential practical use of these new Gibbs states is in developing novel encryption methods. The presence of multiple magnetization levels in these states creates an opportunity for utilizing thermodynamic perturbations to switch spins, thus enabling potential cryptographic techniques. Similarly, the existence of periodic Gibbs states could be leveraged to develop encryption methods, such as one-time pads, utilizing the system's periodicity. These ideas are speculative at the moment, but they are worth pursuing, as they may facilitate the development of highly secure cryptographic tools. The existence of weakly periodic Gibbs states also raises questions about the adequacy of current definition frameworks for Gibbs states, as these states demonstrate a periodicity that is both intrinsic and non-extendable to non-periodic systems. This may prompt experts to broaden the definition of Gibbs states, incorporating additional characteristics. The analysis also sheds light on the interplay between thermodynamic and statistical properties of the system, particularly its magnetization energy. By examining the system's energy at specific temperatures, we were able to identify not only the transition points but also the relative stability of different Gibbs states. This was achieved by evaluating the system's energy at specific temperatures, using the periodization technique to analyze thermal behavior. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to Japanese term segmentation. Given that LSTM neural networks excel at processing sequence data and capturing long-range dependencies, they are ideally suited for addressing the challenges posed by Japanese term segmentation. When handling Japanese terms, character frequencies and meanings are often highly disparate, resulting in poorly correlated character frequencies and lengths. Furthermore, the structure of Japanese terms is complex and varies greatly. For instance, the average length of character sequences in Japanese terms ranges from 2 to 20 characters. To date, Japanese term segmentation has been tackled using Markov models and Conditional Random Fields. Notwithstanding their success, these models are limited to capturing local dependencies and are ill-equipped to handle longer-range dependencies. In contrast, LSTM neural networks are specifically designed to address the challenges posed by sequence data featuring long-range dependencies. In this study, an LSTM neural network is applied to Japanese term segmentation by representing each character as a word vector. The use of word vectors enables the capture of character-level relationships, whereas the LSTM module captures the sequential dependencies inherent in Japanese term sequences. The resulting model was evaluated using ten widely-used Japanese corpora, yielding outstanding results and outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, the use of LSTM neural networks has been advocated as a robust solution to Japanese term segmentation in recent years. However, the research presented here offers several novel contributions: the use of LSTM neural networks for Japanese term segmentation was first explored in Cui et al. (2017), wherein the authors employed LSTM neural networks as a character-level recurrent neural network for Japanese term segmentation. In contrast, the research presented here diverges from earlier work in several key respects: the use of LSTM neural networks was based on a character-based word vector representation, whereas the authors of Cui et al. (2017) employed an LSTM neural network as a character-level recurrent neural network for Japanese term segmentation. Moreover, the research presented here captured the sequential relationships inherent in Japanese term sequences using an LSTM neural network, thus offering a more comprehensive Japanese term segmentation implementation. In summary, the research presented here offers several novel contributions, including the first application of an LSTM neural network to Japanese term segmentation using a word-vector-based representation. Furthermore, the research presented here outperformed existing state-of-the-art techniques, thereby affirming the efficacy and robustness of LSTM neural networks as a comprehensive solution to Japanese term segmentation. Despite the pressing need for climate action, creating and implementing climate policies remains challenging.
A key obstacle is the difficulty for stakeholders to make informed decisions due to the complex and diverse nature of climate information.
A crucial enabler of informed climate action is access to a comprehensive and structured knowledge base on climate-related topics.
Such a knowledge base would standardize climate terminology, facilitate information retrieval, and enable data analysis, ultimately generating insights and guiding climate discussions.
However, developing a climate knowledge base is hindered by the lack of established climate vocabulary and the abundance of unstructured and diverse climate data from the literature.
A Climate Knowledge Graph was proposed to address these challenges by establishing a network of climate entities and their relationships, utilizing Natural Language Processing and the Climate Vocabulary to extract and connect relevant climate information.
The Climate Knowledge Graph can then generate insights and answer climate-related queries, ultimately supporting climate dialogue and informing climate-related discussions.
This research presents an update on the Climate Knowledge Graph's development and its utility in responding to climate questions, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Climate Knowledge Graph in providing insights and guiding climate discussions. 
The Climate Knowledge Graph's knowledge base and climate models are made available for download or access through a cloud-based interface, enabling further reuse and modification by the climate community. 
Future developments will involve integrating the Climate Knowledge Graph with decision support systems, enabling users to navigate the climate knowledge base and generate insights through interactive climate dialogues. 
Additionally, the Climate Knowledge Graph will be applied in other tasks, such as identifying and prioritizing climate interventions, and informing climate-related discussions through relevant knowledge retrieval. 
These and other climate applications will leverage the Climate Knowledge Graph's unique capabilities, ultimately supporting climate action and decision-making. 
The project website serves as a hub for information on the Climate Knowledge Graph, including download links, user guides, and updates on the climate knowledge base and graph models. 
The Climate Knowledge Graph's GitHub repository contains the code used in this research, including the climate vocabulary builder, climate entity extraction, and insight generation. 
The project has benefited from community contributions and participation, inviting the climate community to build upon this work and utilize the Climate Knowledge Graph in addressing pressing global challenges. 
The climate knowledge base and graph can be tailored to meet specific knowledge and graph needs, utilizing the Climate Knowledge graph's knowledge representation and models.

These notes are riddled with inconsistent spelling, abundant abbreviations, and patient-specific information. Current systems focused on extracting symptoms from these notes struggle to adapt their knowledge to different hospitals. This research introduces an effective method to address two key problems - symptom extraction and generalizing across different institutions. First, we standardize the spelling and abbreviations of symptoms using a comprehensive database. Second, we employ a neural network that is trained to recognize patterns across various hospitals, but unlike existing approaches which focus on eliminating noise, ours actually ignores it in favor of capturing essential features. This noise-filtering technique is shown to significantly enhance generalization capabilities in extractive text tasks. Our method demonstrates superior performance in extracting symptoms from unstructured clinical notes when compared to existing systems. Firstly, it addresses the widely acknowledged challenge of sparse rewards in real-world scenarios. Secondly, it tackles the issue of insufficient training data, a critical problem given the need for autonomous driving generalization. Thirdly, it addresses the lack of a comprehensive autonomous driving dataset. Finally, to ensure safe driving, it incorporates rule-based elements into the deep reinforcement learning method. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our solution in navigating complex routes with minimal intervention. Our study also showcases the significance of combining deep reinforcement learning with rule-based actions and novel approaches in handling sparse rewards and limited data. This research presents a novel, effective, and generalizable solution to autonomous driving, resolving three critical challenges in the process. A comprehensive autonomous driving dataset is also made available for public use. Additionally, the developed models and associated codes are accessible on GitHub. Mobile devices' widespread adoption has led to an explosion in demand for intelligent, user-friendly interfaces capable of streamlining productivity and enhancing quality of life through accessible personal assistant functionality. The development of natural language-enabled personal assistants like Google Assistant, Apple Siri, and Amazon Alexa has made significant progress in achieving these goals. Although these assistants can perform a variety of tasks, such as setting reminders, providing sumptuous recommendations, and enabling voice control of the world around us, they still fall short in one crucial aspect - accessing your device's physical capabilities, such as its sensor data. Furthermore, personal assistants currently available are tethered to specific ecosystems (Google, Apple, Amazon) and are inaccessible on older devices due to compatibility issues. To address these limitations, we present Pando, a personal assistant system, built on TensorFlow and JavaScript, that enables voice control of your device's sensor data and integrates seamlessly with existing browsers and speech recognition technologies. The Pando assistant is designed to be versatile, compatible with a wide range of devices, and is characterized by its lightweight architecture and efficient performance. Our experimental results demonstrate Pando's ability to outperform competing assistants in terms of accuracy and speed. Ultimately, our innovative approach sets a new standard for personal assistant technology, and we believe that Pando marks a significant breakthrough in leveraging AI, web technologies, and sensor data to enhance human experience. Our contributions can be utilized to develop a personalized AI experience for your browser, and we are excited to empower the next generation of innovative applications.
