We investigate the impact of T-duality on a twistorial cylinder in six-dimensional supergravity, examining the role of polyforms in this space. These cylinders feature axionic fields and a self-dual two-form derived from a six-dimensional metric. Employing a method similar to bulk-to-boundary mapping, we derive a novel expression for the T-dual metric and an associated self-dual two-form within the cylinders. These forms transform in accordance with T-duality transformations, specifically under $\mathrm{T}^4$ and $\mathrm{T}^2$ transformations. Furthermore, the existing link between topological T-duality and the Poisson-Lie group $\mathrm{T}^3$ is generalized to a six-dimensional framework, establishing novel connections related to the Bruhat decomposition. Additionally, we discover that the root system corresponding to the Poisson-Lie group $\mathrm{T}^4$ is formed by the four-dimensional nilpotent orbit's Bruhat decomposition. We also demonstrate the establishment of a correspondence between the dual space of the Lie algebra and the space of closed one-forms on a twistorial cylinder. This correspondence holds for various levels of nilpotency within the Lie algebra and its dual. Consequently, the correspondence extends to the projection of the polyform onto its core part, bearing resemblance to a Koszul-type duality. Lastly, we show that a specific class of solutions in six-dimensional supergravity, described as holomorphic bundles with connections, are invariant under topological T-duality when the base lies within a nilpotent orbit. These invariant solutions are found to be associated with the algebraic torus $\mathrm{T}^3$ and its dual. Moreover, we discover that a specific class of twistorial cylinders can be expressed as marginal deformations of free hypermultiplets, an understanding achieved through the application of a marginal deformed non-commutative superspace framework. These marginal deformations are shown to be equivalent to the establishment of a self-dual two-form in six-dimensional space. Finally, the established deformations are found to be invariant under the effect of topological T-duality. These results provide a foundation for future research aimed at solving classically invariant challenges in six-dimensional supergravity when the target space lies within a nilpotent orbit. These issues include the establishment of a self-dual two-form, defining twist-dual metrics, and establishing connections between these two forms through braiding. These queries hold at both the general level and when the base lies within a nilpotent orbit

Efficient imitation learning can significantly reduce manual labeling efforts required to train robotic tasks. However, current methods often rely on expert input, which can be costly and time-consuming to obtain. This study introduces a novel approach called co-imitation training, leveraging collaborative expert and student performance data to bypass the need for expert demonstrations. The goal is to achieve comparable results without incurring the associated expenses. To achieve this, co-imitation training unifies diverse policies through a collective experience pool and implements a novel loss function that differentiates student performance variations resulting from different policies, rather than reproducing identical actions. The study includes evaluations of various policies, including random policies and those generated using prior experience, and demonstrates that co-imitation training enables the creation of compatible policies with expert performance quality without requiring expert demonstrations. Moreover, the study shows that these compatible policies exhibit greater diversity than traditionally trained imitators. The study's findings also suggest that the quantity of cumulative experience, rather than the number of involved experts or specific policy distributions, is a crucial factor in determining imitation performance quality. The study's discoveries indicate that co-imitation training offers a versatile and efficient solution to reducing expert demonstration costs in imitation learning. Future research can utilize the findings to broaden the study's scope, which was centered on binary robotic tasks, to address a range of challenges in robotics and beyond. Previous research on PAC codes has focused on binary channels and used non-constructive methods to establish code existence theorems. This study introduces new metrics that can be used to evaluate PAC code performance and provides a method for constructing these codes. We examine PAC code error probabilities and develop a criterion for determining optimal PAC code rates. We also investigate decoding strategies for minimal and optimal PAC codes on binary channels, and we determine the probability distributions of PAC code errors and metrics. Building on this research, we introduce erasure-predictive PAC codes, a new class of PAC codes that can handle multiple, independent channel errors. We achieve this by modifying the traditional PAC code construction method to incorporate an error-predictive metric, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical results. Specifically, we show that EP-PAC codes can predict arbitrary channel errors and achieve superior performance compared to previous PAC code designs. We also investigate the minimum distance between EP-PAC code parity-check matrices and find that this property correlates strongly with optimal PAC code rates. As a result, EP-PAC codes can be employed as an alternative to traditional PAC codes, and they achieve superior performance due to their enhanced error-predictive metrics. We also investigate the EP-PAC code energy spectrum and achieve a geometric analysis of the EP-PAC code Paradise. Based on real-time point cloud data, a suitable coordinate system is selected from the database and used to calculate the end-effector's position by adjusting the camera's orientation. This method can quickly estimate the end-effector's position with an error margin of 2 cm. A simplified algorithm has also been derived that utilizes a depth camera's intrinsic parameters, resulting in accurate position estimates with an error margin of 5 mm. Experimental findings verify that the estimated positions are comparable to the actual values with an average error margin of 1.7 cm. A publicly accessible video showcase has been set up to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. A mathematical representation of this method is presented in this paper, along with associated code that can be accessed via the provided link. This pipeline leverages the Ngmix software as a starting point and incorporates several customization, data preparation, and data validation steps to ensure high-quality results. This includes regions impacted by strong planetary sources, as well as areas near detector edges and known systematic problem areas. This generalizes known results for surfaces and varieties of dimension three. We've discovered that in a specific Heisenberg spin system called the Ce$_2$Mn$_3$Al$_{10}$ magnet, the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition can be adjusted using an external magnetic field. Due to a unique temperature-dependent angle between nearby spins, the transition shifts towards higher temperatures as the field increases. This change is reversible and can be reversed by altering the spin orientation. This unusual Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition is caused by an easily controllable spin anisotropy that also leads to pronounced long-range order at higher temperatures, resulting in an elongated temperature range for the superfluid-like magnetic phase. Using advanced time- and spin-resolution, we've observed the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition and measured the critical temperature under variable magnetic field conditions, confirming our theoretical expectations. This unique phenomenon presents a new pathway for realizing field-tunable quantum phases in systems made of multiple interacting spins. Our study also sheds light on the spin and magnetic motion within Ce$_2$Mn$_3$Al$_{10}$ and sets a new standard for controlling magnetic phases using external fields. This research opens up new avenues for exploring magnetic phenomena and might be applied to other materials with similar properties. Ultimately, adjusting the critical temperature could lead to groundbreaking innovations in magnetic technology and scientific research. Our research focuses on the requirements necessary to replicate BBN neutrino data. As a result, we find suitable mass windows for sterile neutrinos and axions, which align with the QCD axion hypothesis's stability conditions. This research explores a new model of dark energy known as the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, built upon the principles of the Essential model. A crucial component of this model involves the $\bar{\rho}_{D}$ parameter, which is derived from the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological constant and is linked to the radius of a confining sphere in the AdS space. As the Essential model itself experiences difficulties due to its scalar field-based roots, this Tsallis modulated Essential model is further developed using a complex scalar field, thereby addressing the aforementioned challenges. We investigate the cosmological implications of this model by evaluating the equation of state parameter (or EoS) and other key variables, such as the deceleration parameter (or damping factor), Hubble parameter, and fractional variation in scale factor. Notably, our analysis indicates that this model generates a dynamic EoS with no static points, resulting in a transition from a negatively divergent state during early universe periods to a positively divergent state during late universe periods. We also observe that the model's EoS aligns with the screening requirement of the $\bar{\rho}_{D}$ inequality in two distinct regions. Furthermore, we discover that the model's damping factor goes to zero in the late universe, signifying accelerated scale factor growth. Finally, the model's fractional variation in the scale factor is found to be directly proportional to time, indicating that this variation is not a valid approximation for the model's expansion history. These diagrams exhibited remarkable consistency, showcasing regular patterns related to stellar variability, as seen in the CCD images and light curves. Furthermore, the data revealed a significant presence of RR Lyrae variables, with 238 such stars identified across 96 fields, out of which 122 were located in the four $K$ variable plates. In addition, the data included other variable star types, such as RC Cepheids, W Virginis, and SX Phoenicis stars. These findings have significant implications for astronomical research, potentially contributing to accurate measurements of the Milky Way's scale parameter and its local vertical acceleration. Meanwhile, the continued monitoring of these variable stars is anticipated to yield further breakthroughs in understanding celestial objects and their periodic behavior. The security of numerous digital applications heavily relies on high-quality random numbers. True Random Number Generation (TRNG) techniques have been extensively investigated, with many methods exhibiting drawbacks such as elevated power consumption, accelerated chip degradation, prolonged generation times, or limited applicability. This paper introduces TuRaN, a novel approach for generating random numbers that leverages the unique characteristics of SRAM cells in underscaled operation. By reducing the SRAM supply voltage, the adjacent cells' neighboring bit retrievals are demonstrated to produce random data with significant entropy. TuRaN's prototype, built using Graz University's SRAM PUF test chip, successfully passes the NIST standards for random number generation, generating up to 1 million random bits per second at a 100 MB/s write bandwidth without incurring additional power consumption or generating heat. TuRaN operates within an SRAM voltage range of 260 mV to 400 mV, making it a highly efficient and practical method for generating random numbers. This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho theory for baryons with two distinct quark models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition between neutsrons and quarks. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun. Additionally, this research reconstructs the KMT and PJM models in the SOR theory and investigates how the choice of these models affects hybrid star properties. These reconstructed models result in identical behavior for hybrid stars, yet differ in pure hadron stars, prompting concerns about potential inconsistencies. In contrast, we find that the presence of water in sulfuric acid clusters reduces the impact of tunneling on their geometry. Our results suggest that the magnitude of zero-point vibrational motion is substantial, reaching up to 20% of the classical equivalent. Furthermore, we find evidence of level crossing in the potential energy surface of sulfuric acid dimers as a function of quantum-averaged bond length, a phenomenon that largely disappears when tunneling is accounted for. Our findings highlight the necessity of considering tunneling in the study of small sulfuric acid clusters. Since many atmospheric sulfuric acid nucleation studies involve similar systems, we expect our results to hold significant practical implications. Finally, we provide a simple recipe to accelerate the convergence of molecular dynamics trajectories by increasing the mass of virtual particles as the temperature decreases. This mass modification does not affect the dynamics of the atoms themselves but influences the dynamics of the momentum distribution of the virtual particles. Consequently, it leads to the generation of quantum-corrected structures with fewer time steps than trajectories with equally spaced time increments. This method is particularly useful when the time step is larger than the average half-life of the atoms in question. Demographic changes, influenced by past social conditions, lead to variations in the number of opportunities available to different groups, resulting in a self-perpetuating cycle of limited life chances. We applied this idea to racial and ethnic groups and estimated the degree of social investment using historical data on degrees and intergenerational social mobility. We concluded by highlighting the significance of understanding opportunity dynamics in efforts to address social inequalities and promote social mobility. It is essential to recognize the variability in degrees awarded to different groups as a means of social investment, as well as a potential source of disparity in life chances. Focusing on specific scenarios involving mixed states and pure states, we establish strict bounds on the achievable success and failure rates for specific quantum systems, including qubits and qutrits. These rigorous limits are subsequently used to examine the efficacy of certain quantum state transformation methods, including decoherence and the implementation of unitary operations via probabilistic quantum computation. Our study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the optimal application of probabilistic operations in quantum state manipulation. These findings have far-reaching implications for leveraging probabilistic physics for quantum information processing tasks. We begin by defining the basic principles of probabilistic physics and the associated metric for comparing quantum states. We then delve into our findings, starting with the analysis of minimal success rates for local transformations of pure states on multiple-qubit systems. We analyze the optimal approach to combining multiple operations in quantum state distillation, before investigating the maximal failure rates for local pure-state unitary operations. We conclude by examining the applicable range of our bound and its practical implications. These findings open up new avenues for integrating stochastic physics in quantum information processing. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a force that causes oscillations about the equilibrium point, resembling a forced pendulum motion. This resulted in two types of movements: circular and rotational oscillations. The system exhibited two possible responses: stable, small-amplitude motions or chaotic, large-scale movements that can lead to coffee spilling. We analyzed how the initial conditions and force frequency interact to produce these outcomes, identified key parameters that influence stability, and confirmed our findings through experimental measurements in everyday cups. The resulting stability diagram shows the possible responses as a function of driving frequency and amplitude of excitation, observed in our experiments. This research provides insight into the everyday phenomenon of coffee spilling and offers potential applications in design and engineering to prevent spills. Additionally, we observed that our study is related to other research on planar and complex pendulums, which exhibit anomalous behavior, and suggest avenues for further exploration. Key words: forced pendulum, sloshing, stability, anomalous behavior, design. An experimental setup for studying the movement of a cup of coffee while being carried is described, along with numerical modeling and analysis of the system's response to different initial conditions and excitation frequencies. The resulting stability diagram, obtained through both experimental and computational methods, displays the possible responses to varying excitation frequencies and amplitudes, providing essential insights into the dynamic behavior of the system. We observed that the anomalous behavior of our model, specifically the complex rotation, can be attributed to specific parameters and initial conditions, and offer potential applications in design to prevent spills, based on modifying the system's parameters to produce stable motion. Additionally, we propose avenues for further research, focusing on modifying the system to produce rosetta patterns, investigating the effect of key parameters on the system's stability, and exploring the related phenomenon of slumping, using our model to inform the analysis. In machine learning research, the training of deep learning models using decentralized algorithms over communication-limited networks poses a challenge, particularly when dealing with models that require input data homogeneity. To address this issue, we have developed a new distributionally robust decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent algorithm, effectively robustizing decentralized training in deep learning. By integrating the Draganon and Taiki methods into our decentralized training protocol, we have established communication and convergence efficiency for our algorithm. Furthermore, we have proven its convergence to a neighborhood of the optimal solution under the condition that network communication costs do not grow with iteration numbers. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm yields performance comparable to state-of-the-art centralized training methods and significantly outperforms other decentralized training algorithms, especially in models that require input data homogeneity. Additionally, we have found that increasing communication costs can be mitigated through the use of representation learning. We examine particle production during relativistic nuclear collisions utilizing an approach that combines hydrodynamics with kinetic theory. By supposing that an ideal fluid follows hydrodynamic trends below some critical temperature, and using kinetic theory above this temperature, we simulate numerous collisions. This dual-method approach enables us to separate thermal and non-thermal particle contributions. Notably, for collisions beyond a certain threshold (most notably $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 200 GeV at the RHIC and 5.02 TeV at the LHC), the majority of produced particles arise not from non-thermal mechanisms, but rather from the extensive initial state energy that gives rise to a long-lived hydrodynamic ellipse. This discovery allows us to utilize an simplified hydrodynamic attractor concept to predict thermalized particle yields with considerable accuracy. With this new framework, we modify the current minimum bias analysis of the ATLAS collaboration, and find that it yields results consistent with their findings for $p_T \leq$ 5 GeV, and notably, our simulation predicts a breakdown in mass spectrum trends for $T \leq$ 150 MeV, and also predicts differing trends for different particle species. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between initial energy configurations and resulting particle yields, and find that certain relationships previously observed in minimum bias analyses are indeed inherent to the hydrodynamic response to diverse initial conditions. This includes the relationships between anisotropic flow and particle yield, and between particle yield and the amount of initial octupole asymmetry. Lastly, we investigate the connection between collision pressure and the number of produced particles, and find that this relationship is not a result of hydrodynamics "freezing out," but rather a straightforward effect of thermalization. Ultimately, our simulation predicts a total production of NLO, DO, Ks, pi0, eta, and lambda hadrons at the LHC, but still falls short of predicting the observed production of charged particles. To close, we speculate that a future iteration of our thermalization procedure could potentially incorporate non-thermal contributions that fill the remaining predictatory gap. If such an iteration were to be completed before the publication of our abstract, the prediction gap may disappear, and with it, the notable prediction gaps in our Figure 7 may vanish, revealing a new, previously unobserved pattern in the mass spectrum at high $p_T$. This potential advancement could potentially be completed by quantifying non-thermal contributions that fill the prediction gap, and we therefore refer to our full simulation as a "hydrodynamic foundation"

The influence of solar radiation pressure on the dynamics of small orbiting objects has become a critical area of study due to potential disruptions in existing spacecraft missions and the potential impact on the stability of geostationary orbits. A key phenomenon to model this interaction is the solar radiation pressure gradient force, which creates resonances that can significantly impact the movement of small objects within specific orbits. In this study, we establish an analytical model to identify and characterize the semi-secular resonances triggered by the variation in solar radiation pressure, utilizing a Birkhoff normal form approach and valid for a wide range of orbits. Numerical simulations are conducted to analyze scenarios where a small object's motion is confined to specific, predefined orbits, and we examine how its trajectory is affected by variations in solar radiation pressure. These variations cause the object's motion to shift, potentially placing it near resonant positions, where its behavior is largely influenced by the Birkhoff normal form model. Additionally, we explore scenarios involving close encounters between small objects and the Moon, which can amplify the impact of solar radiation pressure on their movement. Specifically, we examine scenarios involving close encounters with the Moon's subtlerodes, which can increase the likelihood of the object becoming trapped in a geosynchronous orbit. In these situations, we find that solar radiation pressure can significantly alter the object's eccentricity, potentially trapping it in a geosynchronous orbit by achieving the required eccentricity. These analytical and numerical models provide valuable insights into the impact of solar radiation pressure on small orbiting objects, which can inform the maintenance and deployment of spacecraft in geosynchronous orbit. Furthermore, they offer potential applications in the field of space mission design, which could be revised to account for the influence of solar radiation pressure. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of the complex interactions between solar radiation pressure, orbiting objects, and gravitational forces, which is essential for maintaining a stable environment in space around Earth. Specifically, we analyzed the influence of solar radiation pressure on specific orbits, which led to new findings and perspectives on predicting the movement of small orbiting objects. Additionally, this research could be applied to develop new methods for predicting the movement of small orbiting objects, which is crucial for existing and future spacecraft missions in geosynchronous orbit. By applying analytical and numerical models, this research offers a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between solar radiation pressure and the movement of small orbiting objects, which is essential for space mission design and management. Furthermore, this research contributes to the development of a stable environment in space around Earth

We investigate how the spatial reflection symmetry in a atomic tight-binding model, that describes light-matter interactions, impacts its eigenvalues. By examining the boundary conditions imposed on wave functions, we determine the measures of discrete and continuous spectra, and subsequently generalize these findings to the study of light-matter interactions. Our analysis reveals that the spectrum of the Hamiltonian is symmetric with respect to the wave number, but not necessarily with respect to the energy. This invariance under spatial reflection is lost when the atomic positions are irregular, and we quantify the degree of incompleteness in the atomic tight-binding model through the violation of this invariance. Our study also extends to the examination of Rabi models that couple atomic states with light fields, and we find that the boundary conditions on photonic eigenfunctions introduce a non-trivial degree of non-hermiticity. Based on these findings, we suggest using approximate self-hermitian reductions of the atomic tight-binding model to model light-matter interactions. Our study offers a framework for generalizing the invariance of light-matter interactions, and potentially applying this invariance in the modeling of metasurfaces. Additionally, the study provides a theoretical basis for the approximation of non-hermitian Rabi models with a finite number of coupled channels. Furthermore, the investigation sheds light on the non-hermiticity of models representing photonic and phononic metasurfaces, and indicates possible losses of completeness in these systems. Finally, the analysis suggests that the approximation of self-hermitian Rabi models could facilitate the reduction of losses of completeness in the optical domain. Ultimately, the investigation offers a theoretical understanding of generalized invariances in light-matter interactions, and the possibility of approximating self-hermitian models will be a subject of future research. Additionally, the study can be extended by considering more complex space symmetries, and the examination of boundary conditions will be a topic of future investigation. In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active calibration problem arises when variables essential for proper perception, such as object pose and form, are unaccounted for in initial predictions. For instance, predicting a centerline from image data alone is insufficient for determining a complete object shape, highlighting the need for additional cues. Furthermore, real-world data often includes noisy and uninformative sensor readings that compromise object detection and perception. Despite these challenges, detecting essential categories is vital for numerous applications across various domains, necessitating the development of enhanced methods capable of producing reliable category-level outcomes. To address the problems mentioned above, we present an iterative refinement approach, dubbed Category-level Object Pose and Form Estimation (COFFEE), designed to optimize object perception by leveraging both 2D and 3D semantic keypoints and image data. By employing a novel graph-based optimization module, COFFEE synergistically combines keystone data, corrects pose and form biases, and produces robust results, all while accounting for potential sensor noise and missing data. COFFEE's efficacy is demonstrated through rigorous testing on real-world datasets and categories, resulting in superior outcomes compared to existing alternatives. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark, referred to as Category-level Object Pose and Form datasets (COPFD), comprising 83 categories commonly found in daily life and totaling over 158K images and 40K poses. These datasets cater to various sensing challenges, offering a comprehensive resource for developing robust category-level perception algorithms. By addressing the unexplored issues of optimal and robust category-level perception, COFFEE and COPFD enable enhanced object detection and perception across diverse domains, enabling automated systems to seamlessly integrate sensing data and producing reliable outcomes under real-world conditions. Code and dataset are openly accessible on our website. The Cauchy distribution, characterized by a singular probability density function, poses calculation difficulties, particularly in determining variance and constructing traditional statistical intervals. This study develops formulas for the mean and variance of Cauchy samples and uses them to establish the formulas for the length of confidence intervals and the square of confidence intervals for the mean of Cauchy distributions. Numerical simulations demonstrate the reliability of these intervals on normal data. Furthermore, these results are extended to estimate parameters in the parameterized form of Cauchy distributions. The proposed methods are compared with alternative techniques, such as the intercept method and Bayes estimation using a uniform prior, in a real-world application involving wind speed data analysis. The simplicity and efficiency of the proposed mean estimation and interval methods are demonstrated through numerical calculations. The work presents a step-by-step mathematical analysis of the techniques in an appendix. The Cauchy distribution's unique nature leads to singular points in its probability density function and a lack of defined moments, making conventional statistical analysis challenging. This study overcomes this limitation by examining the behavior of Cauchy samples and determining the mean and variance of the samples, which are denoted as $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$. The study uses these parameters to establish the formulas for the length of confidence intervals for the mean of Cauchy distributions and the square of confidence intervals, providing a measure of variability. The interval lengths are represented as $L(x,n)$ and the square intervals as $S(x,n)$, where $x$ is the estimate and $n$ is the sample size. The work presents a comparison of these intervals with existing methods, such as the equal-width intercept method, which places equal-length intervals on both sides of a fixed point, and Bayes estimation using a uniform prior. A numerical evaluation of the efficiency of the proposed mean estimation and interval methods is performed through simulations on normal data. The study also applies these intervals to analyze the wind speed data collected at Harwich Port. A new statistical approach assesses sufficient sample sizes required for basket trials comprising various subsets of patients. This method allows clinicians to tailor clinical trials according to disease subtypes defined by genomic characteristics and assess multiple treatments on multiple subtypes simultaneously. Our statistical approach utilizes Bayesian principles to determine the required sample sizes needed for basket trials involving multiple subtypes and sample sizes allocated to each subtype. This is achieved by simulating the trial outcomes in advance and calculating event rates, further incorporating uncertainty related to treatment effects through a posterior distribution. The goal is to balance accurate type I errors and efficient type II errors, ultimately reflecting our level of certainty about treatment benefits. This method applies to the following types of basket trials: genomic-based basket trials and platform basket trials. Our findings show that sample size assessments for basket trials often necessitate enrolling more patients than traditional single-arm or parallel-group trials due to statistical power losses resulting from statistical testing and multiple comparisons. However, basket trials can be more efficient than running individual trials in different subtypes due to the sharing of patients and statistical information. The approach is then illustrated using examples from actual basket trials. Overall, this method provides a useful tool for clinicians and statisticians to plan basket trials by determining the required sample sizes and testing hypotheses on treatment benefits in specific subtypes of patients. By modifying our approach, the method can be extended to incorporate other features of basket trials. The R code for the simulations is available by contacting the corresponding author. To meet the increasing demands of high-throughput and high-precision in advanced motion systems, a novel linear parameter varying (LPV) based sequential loop tightening approach is proposed. It aims to improve the disturbance rejection capabilities and reduce vibration in motion-controlled systems. A specific system, known as the galvanometer, is used as a testbed to demonstrate the efficacy of this technique in enhancing the dynamic performance. Furthermore, a method called sequential loop tightening is presented as an extension of the traditional loop tightening strategy, capable of achieving enhanced high-frequency precision via sequential activation of sensitive parameters in feedback loops. A linear parameter varying model is first identified for the galvanometer, followed by the design of a robust H∞ controller based on LPV loop tightening. Experimental results demonstrate a substantial enhancement in movement precision, specifically a reduction of up to 85% in position error at speeds higher than 1 m/s. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In the context of generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups $G_{m,n}$ and their nilpotent quotients $G_{m,n}^{ab}$, we identify the $R_\infty$-properties. Additionally, we determine which automorphisms of these groups generate twisted conjugacy classes. This involves computing the Burnside ring and the equivariant $K$-theory of $G_{m,n}^{ab}$. Our results are further illustrated by examining specific examples of nilpotent quotients of $G_{m,n}$. We also consider the generalized dihedron group $G_{m,n}^{(r)}$ and the asphericizer of its nilpotent quotient. In the process, we describe the twisted conjugacy classes of self-homeomorphisms of the M\"obius band with a fixed homotopy class of lifts. This involves computing the $K$-theory of the M\"obius band's classification ring. Our findings are supplemented with a comprehensive list of all known instances of group twisted conjugacy classes. To better understand the nature of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ resonances, distribution profiles of electromagnetic form factors are computed for these particles. These profiles are derived from Bethe-Salpeter wave functions generated by Lagrangean models of interaction, specifically the instanton-induced interaction. The results obtained from the models suggest that $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ have a quark-antiquark structure dominated by a compact molecular component, characterized by the quarks sharing the momentum. This is evident in the distribution profiles of the square of the electromagnetic form factor as a function of Bjorken $x$. Additionally, the presence of a long-range quark-antiquark interaction does not significantly alter the distribution profiles, implying that the quark-antiquark correlation due to the interaction is not affected by the separation between the quark and antiquark. A comparison of these findings with experimental data is also presented. Although a comparison with the distribution profiles of the $f_2(1270)$ and $\sigma$ resonances is not directly shown, the quark-antiquark contribution to these particles can be inferred from the results presented here. Based on these quark distribution profiles, it can be assumed that the quark-antiquark component of these resonances also exhibits a compact structure. Therefore, the quark-antiquark component of these resonances likely undergoes a transition to a molecular state due to the interaction, similar to $D^*$ and $D^*_s$. In contrast, the quark distribution profiles of mesons not comprising a quark and an antiquark (such as the $\phi$) are unaffected by the interaction, as expected. A notable observation from these results is that the instanton-induced interaction has a distinct effect on the quark distribution profiles of resonances that can be described as quark-antiquark systems. These results further highlight the importance of instanton-induced interactions in understanding the quark structure of these particles. Current state-of-the-art medical image segmentation methods heavily rely on paired datasets which are often time-consuming and expensive to create. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new unsupervised image segmentation technique called cyclic division GAN, based on non-parallel image division methods. This novel approach allows multiple images to be automatically divided into distinct regions without the need for paired labels. We tested our proposed method using MRI and CT data and observed significant improvements over existing single-modality unsupervised image segmentation techniques. Notably, our method achieved lower Dice similarity coefficients errors of 12.8% and 10.7% for MRI and CT SE sequences, respectively. A visual examination of our results confirms the segmentation quality and highlights the method's ability to produce accurate, visually appealing segmentations. We have released our code and experimental data to allow for replication of our methods and results. Future research directions are also identified. Based on our findings, we believe that CDGAN produces segmentations with reduced gradient error and visually appealing results, making it a suitable technique for performing medical image segmentation using multiple modalities without paired labels. The spectrum of white-light stellar flares observed near ultraviolet wavelengths is not well understood and developing accurate simulations in this range remains a challenge. By using a modified version of the Canuto-Meyer flux distribution, a new formulation is presented to compute stellar flare continua in the near ultraviolet portion of the spectrum. This model is then applied to analyze a notable flare observed in the star AD Leo in 1985, and the resulting flare spectrum exhibits good agreement with actual observations in the wavelength interval of approximately 300 to 330 nanometers. This alignment is achieved by incorporating empirical considerations into the theoretical model, specifically by incorporating photospheric plasma recombination continuum emissions and incorporating observations at longer wavelengths to set a baseline for flux levels. Additionally, the simulations reveal that spatially localized energy release mechanisms, such as the direct heating of trailings layers, play a significant role in explaining the peculiar shape of the flare light curve at shorter wavelengths. This model enhances our ability to interpret space-based observations of white-light stellar flares in the Hubble Space Telescope and the Gaia Photometric System. This model also paves the way for accurate simulations of flares in various cool stars through adjustments to parameterize energy release and heat transfer mechanisms tailored to each specific stellar type. Lastly, the applications of this model could contribute to understanding flare-related effects on extrasolar planets and the variability of stellar energy output that may impact life-supporting planets in the future. The proposed model has the potential to facilitate further research in this area by providing necessary theoretical groundwork. Neural network-based point cloud models have reached a high level of accuracy in handling a wide range of natural and manufactured objects. Despite significant advancements, these models still struggle with the task of learning and predicting object shapes in the presence of missing or ambiguous data. A novel technique, TPC, is proposed to enhance the robustness and reliability of these models by filling in gaps and repairing defects through a data transformation method. TPC utilizes a sequence of geometric transformations to regenerate and complete incomplete or damaged point clouds. Since the specific sequence of transformations remains unknown, a data-driven approach is employed to derive the underlying shape evolution path off-line, which is subsequently applied to both training and testing datasets to yield consistently effective results. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the superiority of TPC over existing completion methods in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. TPC has been made available on GitHub. It is expected that this technique will contribute to the development of robust and reliable neural point cloud models capable of shaping and transforming objects in various applications. When the measurements are taken, the results are compared, allowing us to determine if bell nonlocality is present, even without using mathematical inequalities. To achieve this, our model uses non-optimal correlation outcomes, essentially disregarding the optimal correlation outcomes that would compromise bell nonlocality's detection. The practical examination of bell nonlocality reveals that the nonoptimal correlation outcomes provide a reliable indication of bell nonlocality's existence, even without using mathematical inequalities in real-world experiments. This practical examination of bell nonlocality serves as an essential tool for understanding the concept and its applications in quantum physics. Our research demonstrates that bell nonlocality's detection is feasible with minimal correlation requirements, potentially making quantum key distribution more resilient to security breaches. Additionally, our research highlights bell nonlocality's potential in understanding quantum black-box computations and quantum prediction inequalities. In summary, our research offers a practical glimpse into bell nonlocality's role in quantum physics, utilizing nonoptimal correlation outcomes to detect bell nonlocality's presence. This work was presented at the American Physical Society meeting in Chicago, Illinois, under the title "Ideal demonstration of Bell Nonlocality without Inequalities from Non-Optimal Correlations." Building on recent findings by Gubler and the first author, it is shown that flat lines correspond to semiperiodic divisors and their preimages under toric maps. This result is applied to analyze the localization of zeta functions of line bundles on toric varieties, expressing the value of the zeta function at any prime as a product of factors, each representing the action of a toric map on a line bundle. Further, explicit formulas for the zeta functions of line bundles on weighted projective lines are derived, confirming conjectures by Bannai, Horimoto, and Saxena. Finally, it is demonstrated that the translation action of the torus on its square extends to the space of divisors, providing a novel interpretation of this action and its quotient. This action, denoted τ, corresponds to the geometric Frobenius and crystalline Frobenius actions on the toric map, and its quotient corresponds to the monodromy and Frob\'{e}nenius map. Crucially, it is shown that flat lines are invariant under τ, resulting in a semiperiodic structure on the quotient. This new perspective offers a systematic approach to studying action quotients of tori and its applications to other geometric scenarios. As a consequence, a periodic line bundle on the projective line can be identified, and its existence resolves a long-standing problem. Additionally, it is shown that a generalization of the Fourier-Mousson map exhibits rationality on the projective line, and its eigenvalue curve can be explicitly determined. Finally, it is conjectured that the rationality of the eigenvalue curve holds universally. This research provides insights into the geometry of the eigenvalue curve, potentially opening new avenues for studying its topology. Lastly, it is observed that the developed methods and conclusions can be extended to studying line bundles on stacky toric varieties, encompassing a broader range of geometric scenarios. Crucially, it is noted that flat lines and localization are key concepts not only in algebraic geometry but also in the arithmetic and topology of toric varieties. This methodology, rooted in data-driven methods, uses time-series data to determine and distinguish dynamic system trajectories after successive disturbances. These trajectories are analyzed to calculate a similarity metric, ultimately driving an agglomerative clustering algorithm to group similar trajectories together. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated by applying it to both a theoretical system and a real-world example, with results verifying the ability to correctly identify and differentiate all relevant clusters. Furthermore, this method's ability to efficiently process and group trajectories of varying lengths, as well as its ability to distinguish systems with vastly different behaviors, is highlighted. In particular, an examination of the state-dependent Urquhart system reveals the ability to successfully identify and differentiate multiple distinct clusters, despite the system's tendency to produce lengthy and interconnected trajectory sequences. Conversely, an evaluation of the state-dependent Chua's circuit system, with its extensive and diverse trajectory sequences, verifies the method's ability to efficiently group these trajectories and distinguish between different dynamic system behaviors. This study explores the fundamental concepts of Leibnizian calculus within three contemporary mathematical frameworks: variable smoothings, differential packages, and subtangents. We examine the three frameworks in detail and utilize a philosophical approach known as the'schema technique' to break down the calculations. This enables us to reconstruct Leibnizian calculus by identifying the inherent properties and operations necessary for the derivation of basic calculus results. Our analysis reveals that the three frameworks are equivalent, yet each has distinct philosophical implications related to the nature of infinitesimal calculus. Furthermore, this research offers a systematic defense of Leibnizian calculus against the criticisms of Euler and others. We also discuss how the subtangent framework can be utilized to address many of the criticisms leveled against Leibniz. In particular, this study addresses the challenges related to the sum of an infinite number of infinitesimals and demonstrates that these concerns are mitigated within the subtangent framework. Additionally, this research examines the relationship between Leibnizian calculi and the intuitive geometrical methods of Newton. We focus specifically on the methods for deriving the circle of differences and the calculation of tangents, which were criticized by Leibniz and subsequently defended in this research. These calculations demonstrate that Leibniz misinterpreted Newton's methods, leading to a false belief that they were based on a 'generating quantity.' However, we reconstruct Newton's methods within the subtangent framework and show that they are actually grounded in a distinct calculus of homologous lines. In contrast to Euler's criticism that Leibnizian calculi are not sufficient for deriving the methods of continuous motion, we derive a method for calculating uniform rates of change using the differential framework and show that it aligns with the methods described in Book 2 of the Principia. Finally, this research addresses the long-standing debate over the 'dx' notation and demonstrates that it can be justified within the subtangent framework. We conclude by highlighting that the subtangent framework is well-suited to addressing the criticisms of Euler and others, as well as the philosophical concerns related to the nature of infinitesimal calculus. Ultimately, this research offers a systematic defense of Leibnizian calculus and demonstrates that it can be reconstructed through a precise analysis of the fundamental concepts and operations of calculus. This research also clarifies the distinct approaches to calculus developed by Leibniz and Newton and shows that they are based on a genuine methodological divergence. This paper revisits and expands the observational semantics in the context of timed systems, focusing on environments with crystalline time flow. We address two key issues: (1) defining the relationship between timed and non-timed behaviours, and (2) identifying the sufficient conditions under which the observational semantics for a timed system unambiguously defines the corresponding notion for its corresponding non-timed system. Our work is applicable to a broad range of models, including (weakly) regular transition systems with and without priorities, as well as (weakly) branching time systems with and without priorities. A key aspect of our approach is the introduction of new syntactic properties, known as time determinism and time composability, which are analyzed in relation to their corresponding operational and temporal characteristics. Ultimately, we establish a range of one-to-one correspondence relationships between the timed and non-timed observational semantics, as well as between various sets defined by different time determinism and time composability properties. Our results are illustrated by example models of (branching) time semantics with and without priorities. We believe that our work will contribute to a deeper understanding of the link between timed and non-timed behaviours, thereby enhancing the coherence of theoretical frameworks in the context of model-based reasoning. In particular, this research is expected to benefit systems with periodically activated clock constraints, which cannot be expressed using the standard branching time formula. Specifically, we consider spaces with constant freeway dimension and constant doubling property. Our findings show that the problem can be solved efficiently using a greedy approach for spaces with constant freeway dimension, but this approach is not effective for spaces with constant doubling property. In particular, we prove that a feasible solution with a limited number of hops can be obtained efficiently, but this result implies that finding an optimal solution is NP-hard for spaces with constant doubling property, even when k is relatively small. Our analysis also reveals that, for spaces with constant doubling dimension, we can obtain an approximate solution with a limited number of hops for the k-Admin Center problem, where the goal is to select k centers such that the largest number of points within a certain distance from its assigned center does not exceed a specified value A. Another problem investigated is finding the minimum number of centers required such that the largest distance from a point to its assigned center does not exceed B, for which we obtain efficient algorithms when the space has a constant freeway dimension and a set of points with at most k associated centers, or with a constant freeway dimension and a fixed number of associated centers. In this paper, we explore improving the solving of polynomial linear systems with noisy measurements by utilizing techniques from approximate computation. By leveraging absolute error propagation and smoothing, we establish tighter bounds for system solving under specific noise conditions. These bounds are more precise than existing estimates, particularly in the low signal-to-noise ratio range. Additionally, we incorporate an early termination method to prematurely halt the solving process if the desired solution's error surpasses an acceptable threshold, enabling a trade-off between computation time and tolerance. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of this method to multiple polynomial products and present experimental results demonstrating its efficacy. These findings are further substantiated by analytical benchmarks, showcasing a notable reduction in computation time across a range of scenarios. Crucially, the early termination method can be utilized before identifying the actual rank of the system's matrix, thereby not affecting the accuracy of the output. We thoroughly examine the influence of system non-homogeneity, noise variance, and degree on termination performance, revealing that a higher degree of non-homogeneity induces an earlier termination due to increased error propagation. Notably, our studies indicate that the worst-case and average termination rates converge asymptotically. We hypothesize that this behavior may be attributed to the system's high-degree non-homogeneous polynomials and the high-degree numerator coefficients, which could benefit from further investigation. To facilitate the integration of approximate solvers into existing polynomial system solvers, we suggest modifying the tolerance and terminating criteria to accommodate random mistakes, thereby requiring only minor modifications to existing code. We illustrate this process with an example using PSLG-BR, a solver for sparse polynomial systems, and present experimental results demonstrating the simplified implementation. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct a comprehensive study featuring 14,951 system instances across various dimensions and degrees, which reveals a notable reduction in computation time while preserving adequate accuracy. Specifically, early termination yields a time savings of up to 93.5% with only a 2% approximation error, and subsequently decreases as the degree of non-h Homogeneity (dNH) increases. We observe that termination occurs at a notably younger node for higher values of dNH, and note an interesting 'S' pattern in our data, which we hypothesize may stem from the inherent characteristics of the system's high-degree non-h Homogeneous polynomials. These findings could benefit from further statistical analysis in a larger dataset. In summary, we have developed an efficient strategy for approximating polynomial linear system solving by incorporating an early termination method that leverages random mistakes and tolerances

We explore a scenario of parity-symmetry-protected two-photon emission from a strongly coupled point dipole in an optically driven system. Our model reveals two mechanisms contributing to this phenomenon: one arising from the dipole's initial state dynamic perturbation, and another from the dipole's transition to a finite-energy virtual state. These two processes yield a resonant emission spectrum characterized by package-like features. Based on a developed theoretical framework, we simulate a situation involving a pyroelectric material coupled to an optical cavity. Our findings indicate that by carefully selecting materials with specific spontaneous polarization and incorporating them into cavities with designated driving fields, it is possible to achieve parity-symmetry-protected two-photon emission with the desired feature pattern. With ongoing research focused on protecting symmetry in the presence of driving fields and to engineering feature-rich emissions, our study contributes to the understanding and development of parity-symmetry-protected photonics. Additionally, exploring artificial systems that exhibit parity protection could provide a pathway to realizing our proposed model using artificial quantum systems. An inverse relationship between the emission spectrum's features and the driving field has been identified, with features becoming more pronounced as the driving field decreases. However, a threshold needs to be reached where features completely vanish, and further decreases in the driving field result in two-photon emission that is no longer parity-protected. Beyond applying parity symmetry in protecting two-photon emission, our model explores the interactions between all three components - the point dipole, the cavity, and the driving field - to identify the emission spectrum's features. As a result, feature-rich two-photon emission could serve as an indicator of a system that is parity-protected. Our research presents a comprehensive understanding of parity-symmetry-protected two-photon emission and features, and we anticipate that our results will contribute to the development of feature-rich and parity-symmetry-protected photonics. Additionally, we find that feature-rich two-photon emission could be achieved by decreasing the driving field or incorporating materials with spontaneous polarization in optical cavities. These understanding and findings could pave the way for exploring artificial quantum systems that exhibit parity protection and for investigating the interactions between all components of a system to reveal its inherent features. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Compared to existing approaches, the proposed model offers enhanced simplicity and precision, with a deviation of less than $0.5\%$ from numerical simulations and linearly decreasing errors with increasing pressure. This concise equation state model facilitates a deep understanding of the alkali metals' physical characteristics and enables calculation of key thermodynamic properties, such as internal energy, specific heat capacity, thermal expansion coefficient, and isentropic expansion work. Moreover, the precise analytical equation state model minimizes the reliance on numerical simulations, thereby enabling straightforward and rapid evaluations of the alkali metals' thermodynamic properties, such as those necessary for engine combustion analysis, where temperature and pressure conditions often extend beyond $10^6$~Pa and $10^4$~K. This concise equation state model, therefore, holds significant value for both low-temperature and high-temperature applications. Moreover, the proposed model's mathematical structure could be adapted for use in modeling the gas phase of pure polyatomic molecules. This potential adaptation is discussed in the presented study. Tables containing calculated thermodynamic properties, along with theoretical vs. Monte Carlo simulation comparisons, are available online at the following address: https://bit.ly/3bS1zYR. We investigate how vector mesons behave in a medium characterized by a chiral imbalance, caused by the vacuum's fermion condensate. A specific model relying on the vector-meson dominance hypothesis and a specific gauge boson representation is used to explore this phenomenon. In this context, we discover that not only does the medium induce a significant modification in the vector meson's effective mass, but it also results in multiple, distinct resonance peaks, in addition to altering the vector meson's transmission and scattering properties. These findings are particularly relevant to the study of charged currents in heavy ion collisions and the phenomena of dual plasmon and a close relation with the Cornwall-Jackiw-Tombrello boson. It is also demonstrated that the complex structure of the vector meson's propagator, influenced by chiral anomalies and Asymmetries, gives rise to distinct physical effects. Lastly, the concept of a Wess-Zumino term is discussed in relation to the vector meson's wetland and scattering coefficients. It is evident that the vector meson's wetland is comprised of three components: the real wetland, a Wess-Zumino term, and a hidden wetland. These components are significantly affected by the chiral imbalance and vector meson coupling. Consequently, the scattering coefficients, mediated by the vector meson, differ notably from the traditional, uncoupled cases. These observations underscore the importance of considering how vector mesons interact with the chiral medium and the resultant, complex wetland structure. It is anticipated that future research will validate these predictions in the context of charged particle collisions. Additionally, the possibility of detecting the vector meson's hidden wetland in the context of a table-top experiment is explored. It is conjectured that the production of a pair of vector mesons at the same energy bin could serve as a landmark indicator of the hidden wetland. Consequently, the detection of such phenomena would not only validate the existing understanding of the wetland structure but also offer a novel perspective on the nature of anomalies and Asymmetries. It is envisioned that future research will uncover the underlying connection between the production of vector meson pairs and the hidden wetland, aided by the chiral imbalance. We examine the problem of accurately estimating a scale parameter in complex networks that are resistant to efficient navigation, under the condition that some data transmitted by network nodes may be unreliable and intentionally manipulated. This unusual scenario is modeled as an information-theoretic problem, for which we establish a fundamental limit on what information can be extracted from data affected by malicious interference. We then devise a reliable estimation method that approaches this limit, relying only on data exchanged between nodes and not requiring any trusted central authority or perfect data shared among nodes. This solution is validated through experiments conducted on both artificially constructed and natural networks. Interestingly, we observe that the reliable estimation method not only recovers the scale parameter but also detects the existence of malicious nodes. Furthermore, applications of our solution are found in both the study of resilient networks and the construction of robust multi-agent consensus algorithms. Ultimately, our work provides valuable insights into what information can be obtained under hostile conditions and paves the way for further exploration into data extraction in the presence of malicious activity. Keywords: Complex networks, Network scale estimation, Byzantine faults, Information-theoretic limits, Reliable estimation, Malicious nodes. JEL Classification: C66, C80. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex gravitational waves, ensuring that the spatial metric remains isotropic and hydrodynamics equations are unaffected, demands that the initial conditions for all degrees of freedom be precisely determined. The conditions for gravitational waves are particularly challenging due to the infinite degrees of freedom resulting from infinitely many wave modes. A key algebraic equation, stemming from the constraint that div(A_f = 0), is notoriously difficult to solve because of its high nonlinearity. This work presents a novel solution method called the Choice of Trial Functions using Koopman operator theory, which simplifies the problem and yields a viable solution across a wide range of states. This method outperforms previous methods, such as the Conjugate Gradient Method, in an explicit test from [1]. A key advantage of this method is its ability to produce multiple valid solutions, allowing researchers to control the spread of the source term. This method is specifically designed for use in (3+1)-schemata and therefore has a range of applications, extending from astrophysical black hole ringdowns to early universe simulations of gravitational waves produced by cosmological perturbations. This method is expected to significantly enhance the accuracy of numerical relativity simulations involving intricate sources of gravitational waves. Details of this method, along with accompanying code, can be found at https://github.com/cttk/CTTK/tree/master-docs. Extended documentation can be found at https://cttk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. A related arXiv paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01475. Related talk can be found at https://youtu.be/6R9R9O5M7mY. Related GitHub issue is https://github.com/cttk/CTTK/tree/master-docs/. This work was influenced by Robert Wald's lectures on "General Relativity at the Crossroads" and Brian van den Brink's "Quantum Mechanics in Three Dimensions". A public Jupyter notebook is available at https://nbviewer.ipython.org/ to illustrate the methods described. It outlines the steps required to obtain the source term in numerical relativity, which can then be input into various regularization methods such as the Hyperplane Method and the Caustic Method, all of which are part of a broader family of techniques known as the Hyperplane Family. Predicting complex time series events in multiple dimensions presents significant challenges, primarily due to difficulties in selecting relevant relevant variables from available data and constructing an optimal model architecture. Our research addresses these obstacles in the context of nonlinear multidimensional time series, focusing on event prediction. We introduce an adaptive graph convolutional network, featuring an optimized variable selection method and an adaptive CNN architecture. Initially, our model selectively chooses temperature and pressure variables from real-time data, before training an adapted CNN to make predictions. Notably, the simplicity of our approach enables seamless integration into existing systems using in-graph and out-graph features. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance of our model over conventional methods, both in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, following extensive cross-validation trials. Ultimately, the proposed approach yields a significant boost in prediction performance, approximately 27.5% better than alternative methods. Consequently, this adaptive graph CNN model is highly suitable for use in time-critical applications involving event prediction, where both precision and efficiency are critical considerations. We further showcase the effectiveness of our model by successfully applying it to monitor and predict events in real-time datasets from operating commercial microelectromechanical systems. This significant enhancement in performance, resulting from integrating the adaptive variable selection method with CNN, is evident across seven different datasets. Specifically, our model outperformed controls by significant margins when predicting events related to capillary leakage, vacuum failure, and turbulent flow, as well as when analyzing data from a pressure sensor and a vibration sensor. These results are presented in detail, along with visualizations of our model's predictive performance. Additionally, we have made the adaptive graph CNN code available for public use via public repositories. This includes a detailed explanation of how to train the model using real-time data, as well as the necessary steps for performing variable selection. Consequently, the adaptive graph CNN model represents a valuable resource for developers, where it can be utilized to boost prediction performance in multidimensional time series applications. Lastly, key areas for future research are identified, focusing on further refining the variable selection method and exploring the integration of recurrent models. These potential research avenues are highlighted, along with their associated challenges, thereby outlining a range of promising research directions in this area. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current ADCs are developed using simplified atmospheric models that don't account for varying dispersion levels across different wavelengths. We've conducted on-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion using a Seismic Accelerometer that can record the varying index of refraction in real-time. We've collected data under different atmospheric conditions in Chile and Argentina, recording the varying index of refraction and corresponding dispersion levels across various wavelength ranges. We've developed a new model that utilizes these measurements, providing a more accurate description of how dispersion changes with wavelength and atmospheric conditions. This model supplements the existing model by accounting for differences in dispersion levels. We've applied our model to measured data, yielding results that match the on-sky measurements with minimal error. This model will facilitate the development of more advanced ADCs that can effectively correct dispersion across various wavelength ranges, from a few hundred to tens of thousands. This model can also be used to improve the design of ADCs using simulation software and optimize their performance. We've collected sufficient data to develop new models for specific atmospheric conditions in different locations, allowing for the development of location- and condition-specific ADCs that can effectively correct dispersion under varying environmental conditions. This research is part of a broader project that aims to develop on-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion, providing data-driven models that can inform the design and improvement of ADCs. This unique data can potentially be utilized in various fields that utilize ground-based telescopes, such as astronomy and seismology. A software tool is currently being developed to rapidly generate custom ADC models based on these data, providing custom-developed ADCs that can effectively correct dispersion under specific atmospheric conditions. These custom ADCs can be applied to a wide range of telescopes, encompassing various types and sizes. Once completed, this resource will be made publicly available. We're collecting and developing these data in response to a widely-held assumption that on-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion aren't feasible due to technical constraints. This assumes that in-situ measurements of the varying index of refraction are too localized, incapable of accurately representing the varying index of refraction across a wider area. However, our results demonstrate that these measurements can, in fact, represent the on-sky conditions with minimal error. The establishment of training data is crucial for the development of academic materials, particularly when multiple instructors are involved in labeling. Typically, their labels are combined to create a single, unified dataset, and then used to develop a comprehensive system. Recently, a new approach, known as multi-instructor labeled distillation, has been explored, in which multiple instructors' labels are utilized to create a robust, pairwise ensemble. However, implementing such technique proves challenging due to the distinct distributions of instructors' labels and the difficulty in computing their respective probabilities. This paper introduces an innovative method, called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), that tackles these issues to effectively distill multi-instructor training data. Our approach iteratively pairs instructors with the highest performance to create an ensemble, using the probabilities derived from logits to improve dependence and representation. PILE is evaluated on various educational datasets, and our experiments confirm its superior performance compared to existing baseline methods. Moreover, our analysis highlights the distinct characteristics of instructors' labels and their relationship with educational content. This study explores how well sparse solutions are represented by their support within a continuous framework for basis pursuit. For a specific inner product space equipped with a continuous basis, we demonstrate that a sparse solution can be uniquely reconstructed from its moments with respect to any arbitrary continuous set that covers its support. Furthermore, our method is adaptable and can be implemented using conventional iterative techniques similar to L1-minimization algorithms. Additionally, we show that enforcing a Lipschitz-continuity constraint on the basis results in representability by a finite basis set, thus providing an alternative approach to existing results. Finally, we discuss how our findings generalize the concept of null-controllability in control theory. However, we also identify a critical limitation - the existence of non-unique representations for differently equipped subspaces of infinite dimension. To address this limitation, we develop a novel "average support" concept that selects a single representative for each collection of mutually exclusive sparse solutions. Consequently, we derive an operator that outputs the unique support for any given inner product with a continuous basis. Our work covers a broad range of applications, and we subsequently apply it to the control of ordinary differential equations and partial differential equations. Lastly, we suggest that our methods and results can be extended to other sparsity-promoting optimization problems. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive theory for the uniqueness of answers in basis pursuit in the continuous context. Leveraging the continuity of representations, we derive novel properties and reflect on the distinct aspects of continuous sparsity. Moreover, we investigate the computability of these properties, particularly in the context of solving partial differential equations with sparse data. To achieve this, we develop an iterative algorithm that outputs a sequence of sets, where each iteration incorporates information from the previous step, ultimately converging to the desired unique support. Moreover, we show that this iteration can be halted and the solution determined within a specified number of steps that depends only on the Lipschitz constant and tolerance, but not the size of the support. This property enables us to sample the basis and compute the unique support using conventional iterative methods. Additionally, we comment on how our results generalize to the discrete case, and the specific conditions under which uniqueness fails. Moreover, we prove that enforcing a Lipschitz constraint on the basis results in representability by a finite basis set. Furthermore, we develop an alternative approach to generalizing the concept of null-controllability in control theory. Lastly, we apply our unique support to the control of ordinary differential equations and partial differential equations, and demonstrate its equivalence to existing methods in simple cases

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison. Our compiler backend supports both standalone execution and table embedding on top of a base P4 program, offering flexibility in application development. A comprehensive validation suite ensures correct functionality and benchmarking tests compare the efficiency of different mapping algorithms. Interestingly, a randomization-based mapping algorithm consistently outperformed or matched the performance of more complex algorithms in resource usage and throughput. The open-source nature of our work enables researchers to leverage our resources to further optimize P416 program compilation for the V1Model architecture. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/openv1model/openv1model-devtools. Additionally, the switch models used in our experiments can be found at https://github.com/openv1model/openv1model-Models. Relevant papers on our work have been published on arXiv, CCRN, and DBLP. A low-order finite element method for simulating vector transport in complex geometries is developed and implemented. Although widely used, standard methods often fail or produce errors due to curved boundaries, singular shapes, or high rates of deformation. Our approach builds on the discrete transport equation by incorporating a stabilising term, thereby ensuring the accuracy and robustness of the simulation. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the method's performance in a variety of normal and pathological cases. These tests demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of the proposed technique. Additionally, a comparison with a related method shows that our approach offers superior results in scenarios involving sharp changes within the vector field. These findings are documented in a report. Further details on the numerical strategy, as well as the underlying theoretical framework, can be found in a companion research paper.
