Optimizing wireless network performance often involves striking a balance between delay, throughput, and energy efficiency. This balance is particularly important in device-to-device (D2D) networks, where increased network scale can exacerbate age of information (AoI), leading to suboptimal performance. To address this challenge, we develop an age of information aware two-stage optimization framework for D2D packet transmission. In the first stage, a deep learning approach is used to create an optimal packet transmission schedule. In the second stage, a binary optimization method is applied to determine active D2D transmitters. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, which outperforms existing solutions and achieves near-optimal performance. Additionally, we find that deep learning schedules can be utilized across various scales of D2D networks. To further investigate the efficiency of our schedule, we examine the difference between scheduled and unscheduled D2D transmissions, and find that the former significantly enhances network communication effectiveness. This observation underscores the importance of transmission scheduling in maintaining efficient D2D communication. Finally, we find that increased D2D network scale can lead to longer average AoI, which serves as a key motivator for optimizing D2D transmission scheduling. Code for replicating the figures in this paper is available at https://github.com/AliRostami/AoI-Based-WD2D-Optimization. Key Words: Age of Information, Wireless D2D, Optimization, Deep Learning, 5G Systems.

The growing presence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in daily life is undeniable, yet its practical applications are hindered by the stigma of reliability concerns. Researchers and developers strive to enhance AI systems' trustworthiness, which often revolves around the explainability of their decisions. Explainability serves as a broad umbrella term encapsulating various AI-related reliability concerns. Requirements engineering plays a crucial role in fostering user-centric AI development, including the incorporation of explainability requirements. We aim to investigate how requirements engineering can contribute to the development of more transparent and understandable AI systems, with a focus on explainability requirements. These requirements are frequently overlooked, yet they play a vital part in addressing users' needs and promoting trust in AI. We seek to identify and distill the key challenges and opportunities surrounding explainability requirements, promote related research and practice, and outline potential future avenues to explore. These areas of focus include establishing a shared understanding of explainability, integrating it with current AI research trajectories, and incorporating explainability requirements in actual development processes. By addressing these questions, we can establish requirements engineering's contribution to developing more understandable and transparent AI systems, ultimately promoting user-centric AI development. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Explainability, Requirements Engineering, Machine Learning, Robot Ethics.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for specific pathological characteristics. Despite the importance of this task, it is largely uncontrollable due to the subjective nature of its current implementation, which relies on experienced pathologists' assessments. In this study, we outline the formation of a large, annotated dataset called UniToPatho, which enables the automation of this process. Comprised of 13,325 stained and H&E-stained histological images, this dataset is specifically designed for the classification of colorectal polyps and adenoma abnormalities. We utilize UniToPatho for evaluations of deep learning strategies for classification and regression tasks, ultimately discovering that a combination of multiple convolutional neural networks can predict adenoma levels with an error rate of 5.48, outperforming traditional convolutional neural networks and ensemble models composed of residual and batch normalization layers. A new hierarchical deep generative model, referred to as MrSARP, is presented in this paper, in which each component learns to generate multiple aspects of a target signal. This model leverages its inherent structure to produce a prior that facilitates image enhancement through a Bayesian learning approach, resulting in the recovery of meaningful details in a degraded image without the need for a reference. To evaluate the effectiveness of MrSARP, a set of experiments was performed under various conditions of noise, saturation, and distortion, in both simulated and real-world environments. The results demonstrate that MrSARP successfully enhances a range of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images by removing saturation-induced distortion, restoring details obscured by noise, and correcting non-uniform distortion without the need for a reference image. In each of these scenarios, MrSARP outperforms existing image enhancement methods in terms of restored image quality. The structure of MrSARP consists of multiple latent variables, each of which represents a distinct aspect of a target signal. One of these variables is responsible for capturing the background of an image, while another generates the foreground or areas of interest. A module within MrSARP known as a encoder-decoder-encoder (EDE) module enhances the coherence of the generated background by first encoding the input image, then generating a background, and finally decoding the generated background to produce the output image. A separate module within this structure, referred to as the cross-modal module, is used to capture the spatial relationships between different aspects of a target signal as well as the relationships between background and foreground. Through the integration of these modules, MrSARP is able to recover degraded areas of a target signal while preserving the coherence of the remaining signal components. A theoretical analysis of MrSARP is provided in this study, in which the likelihood of each component is maximized through an optimization approach. A new model-free reinforcement learning algorithm is introduced, allowing agents to optimize their policies in continuous duration settings. Building upon traditional q-learning, this 'duration q-learning' algorithm addresses the challenge of handling varying task durations, enabling an agent to exploit knowledge gained along the way. Mathematically, the task is reformulated as an optimal control problem with a dual formulation, enabling iteration between policy improvement and fitness evaluation. Empirical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel approach, with successful applications in simulated robotic tasks, specifically reaching targets in 2D and 3D environments, even when initial task durations are unknown. Empirical results confirm that a learned policy remains effective across a range of task conditions. Ultimately, this paper presents a unified framework for reinforcement learning in continuous duration contexts, enabling control of tasks with predictable or unpredictable durations. Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factors, which measure low-energy magnetic oscillations, are typically narrow and peaked, but certain models, like the Hubbard models on triangular and square lattices, yield multiple peaks below a critical temperature. By using high-temperature expansions to study the Hubbard models on these lattices with zero electronic attraction, we observe that multiple peaks in the dynamical structure factors merge into a single broad peak at higher temperatures. We create phase diagrams for these Hubbard models by analyzing high-temperature expansions and calculate critical temperatures.
